title: Extinguishers and gas cylinders — handling, transport and service
activity: Handling, transporting and servicing portable extinguishers and gaseous suppression cylinders: 9 kg and 50 kg units, cylinder removal from a bank, transport in the ute, discharge testing, agent recovery, hydrostatic testing and refilling.

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(f)
hrcw.text: is carried out in or near a confined space

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(i)
hrcw.text: is carried out on or near pressurised gas distribution mains or piping

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(k)
hrcw.text: is carried out on or near energised electrical installations or services

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(l)
hrcw.text: is carried out in an area that may have a contaminated or flammable atmosphere

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(o)
hrcw.text: is carried out in an area at a workplace in which there is any movement of powered mobile plant

whenRequired:
Any day you put a hand on a pressurised extinguisher or a suppression cylinder — the six-monthly and yearly rounds, the five-yearly discharge and pressure test, pulling cylinders out of a gaseous bank, carting them in the vehicle, and filling them in the workshop.

IS THIS HIGH RISK CONSTRUCTION WORK? That is a judgement made per job, not a box already ticked. Make it before you start, and write the answer on the job card.

A round of six-monthly extinguisher checks in an occupied building is ordinarily testing or maintenance of a minor nature under s 289(3)(d) of the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) and falls outside Chapter 6. But do not treat that as a blanket carve-out. s 289(1) expressly names decommissioning, and s 289(2)(e) expressly brings in "the installation, testing or maintenance of an essential service in relation to a structure". A fire suppression system is an essential service. Decommissioning and recommissioning a gaseous bank, pulling cylinders, or leaving a system isolated beyond the visit is not minor work — treat it as construction work and go to s 291.

On this activity the s 291 categories that can apply are listed in the HRCW section of this statement: (f) in or near a confined space, (i) on or near pressurised gas distribution mains or piping, (k) on or near energised electrical installations or services, (l) an area that may have a contaminated or flammable atmosphere, and (o) an area with movement of powered mobile plant. If any of them applies to what you are actually doing today, this is high risk construction work.

WHOSE STATEMENT IS IT? Ours. If this work is high risk construction work, s 299 puts the duty to prepare the safe work method statement on the person conducting a business or undertaking that carries out the work — Safe QLD Fire Protection — and the statement has to meet s 299(2): identify the high risk construction work, state the hazards and risks, describe the control measures, and describe how they are implemented, monitored and reviewed. There is no such thing as a "principal contractor SWMS". Where the work forms part of a construction project — construction work costing $250,000 or more, s 292 — the principal contractor must take all reasonable steps to obtain a copy of this statement before the work starts (s 312), must prepare a WHS management plan (s 309), and must make us aware of its content before we start (s 310). We work to that plan; we do not wait for them to write our statement.

If the same visit means working more than 2 m up, cutting or grinding, or work on the electrical supply side of a panel, that work is not covered here and needs its own statement. Do not stretch this one to cover it.
permits: System impairment / isolation permit from the building manager or the site's fire safety adviser before any suppression system goes to isolate — get the reference number in writing
Monitoring company isolation job number, obtained before the releasing circuit is isolated and quoted again when it is restored
Site permit to work or plant room access permit where the building runs one
Personal danger tag and lock on the releasing isolate switch — your lock, your key, in your pocket

Confined space entry permit under AS/NZS 2865:2009 (Amd 1:2025) where the cylinder bank sits in a pit, tank room or unventilated void that meets the definition — a plant room key is not an entry permit, and the space must be signed at every entry under s 68 of the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld)
Hot work permit under AS 1674.1 if a seized bracket has to be cut or ground — that is separate work under a separate SWMS

Commonwealth extinguishing agent authorisation held by the business before any HFC (FM-200/HFC-227ea, HFC-125, HFC-236fa) or halon agent is acquired, decanted, recovered, stored or disposed of. This is the trading-side authorisation under the Ozone Protection and Synthetic Greenhouse Gas Management Act 1989 (Cth) and its Regulations, and it belongs to the business, not to you. If the office cannot produce it, the agent stays in the cylinder.

Dangerous goods transport documentation and emergency information where the load exceeds the tools-of-trade quantity under the Transport Operations (Road Use Management—Dangerous Goods) Regulation 2018 (Qld)
ppe: Safety glasses to AS/NZS 1337.1, on from the vehicle to the vehicle
Full face shield over glasses for discharge testing, valve removal and charging
Steel cap boots to AS/NZS 2210.3 — a 50 kg cylinder lands on the foot first
Cut-resistant grip gloves for handling; cold-resistant gloves for CO2 horns, valves and discharge lines
Class 5 earmuffs or plugs to AS/NZS 1270 for discharge testing — a CO2 discharge is over 110 dB
P2 respirator to AS/NZS 1716 for dry chemical decant, internal inspection and refill
Chemical splash apron and nitrile gauntlets for wet chemical (potassium salt) and foam decant

Personal gas monitor matched to the agent in the room — an oxygen monitor for nitrogen, argon and inert blends; a CO2 sensor or a multi-gas instrument with a CO2 channel wherever CO2 is stored, discharged or filled. Bump tested before the shift, calibration sticker in date, worn on the collar and not left in the toolbox.

Breathing apparatus staged (not worn) outside the discharge bay and the fill room before any CO2 or inert-gas discharge — the set checked, in date, and a person on the crew trained and fit tested in it. If nobody on the crew is BA-trained, the standby person's only job in a rescue is to call 000 and keep everyone out.
Hi-vis shirt or vest, and hard hat where the site requires it
training: QBCC fire protection occupational licence — Portable, install and maintain (and Portable, certify where the technician signs the record)
QBCC fire protection occupational licence — Special hazard fire system, install and maintain, for any work on gaseous suppression cylinders, actuators or releasing gear

Extinguishing agent handling licence under the Commonwealth scheme for any work that decants, recovers, transfers or disposes of HFC or halon extinguishing agent. This is the licence class dealt with by the Ozone Protection and Synthetic Greenhouse Gas Management (Extinguishing Agent Handling Licences—Qualifications and Standards) Determination 2024 (Cth), made under the Ozone Protection and Synthetic Greenhouse Gas Management Act 1989 (Cth). It is issued for the fire protection industry by the Fire Protection Industry (ODS & SGG) Board — confirm the current licence classes and application route with the office before you apply, and carry the card. A QBCC licence does not cover you for this.

Halon is more restricted again — no halon 1211 or 1301 is decanted, transferred or disposed of without the specific Commonwealth halon permission for that work. If you find halon in a bank, stop and ring the office.
Cylinder filling, inspection and testing competency to AS 2030.5:2026, carried out at a certificated gas cylinder test station working to AS 2337.1-2004
Queensland open driver licence; dangerous goods driver licence only if a placard load is carried
General construction induction card (white card) for construction sites
Site induction and plant room induction for the building
Hazardous manual tasks training covering team lifting and cylinder trolley use
Confined space entry and gas testing to AS/NZS 2865:2009 (Amd 1:2025) where a bank is in a confined space — entrant and standby person both trained, both current

Gas detector use: bump testing, calibration checks, what the alarm points mean and what to do when one sounds. A technician who has not been shown how to bump test the instrument does not carry it as a control.
Breathing apparatus training and fit testing for at least one person on any crew doing a CO2 or inert-gas discharge
High risk work licence class LF where a forklift is used to move cylinder pallets in the workshop
Current first aid and CPR — at least one person on the crew

steps.step: Plan the run and set the vehicle up before anything is loaded
hazards: Turning up with no way to move a 50 kg cylinder
Cylinders loose in a tray with no rated anchor points
Carrying more dangerous goods than the tools-of-trade concession allows
Wrong agent or wrong size brought to site, so the job gets improvised
Arriving at an HFC or halon bank with no recovery unit, so the agent gets vented

controls.control: Service in place wherever the standard allows it. A 50 kg cylinder that does not need the workshop does not get carted to the workshop.
Cylinder trolley with a retaining chain and a wheel brake on the vehicle before it leaves the yard, plus a ramp or tailgate for anything over 16 kg.
Cylinders travel in an upright rack strapped to rated anchor points in a ventilated tray or canopy — never a sealed box, never the passenger cabin.
Read the site's asset register in the app first: type, size, agent, last service and the test date stamped on each shoulder. Load to that list.

If any HFC or halon agent is coming out of a cylinder today, the recovery unit and an empty, in-test recovery cylinder go on the truck before you leave. No recovery gear means the agent stays where it is and the job gets rebooked — it does not get vented to make the day work.

Gas instrument matched to the agent you are going to: oxygen for nitrogen, argon and inert blends; CO2 channel wherever CO2 is stored or discharged. Bump test it at the bench, check the calibration sticker, and do not leave the yard with a flat one.

Count the load against the tools-of-trade limits in the Transport Operations (Road Use Management—Dangerous Goods) Regulation 2018 (Qld). Over the threshold means a DG driver licence, placards and transport documents — check before loading, not at the roadside.
10 kg ABE extinguisher on the vehicle, in date, accessible from the driver's door.

steps.step: Assess each unit before you touch it
hazards: Corroded, pitted or bulged shell letting go under stored pressure
Cylinder that has been in a fire or arc-struck
Damaged valve, bent actuator or stripped neck thread
Unit out of hydrostatic test date
Unknown or mixed agent
Scheduled synthetic greenhouse gas or halon vented to atmosphere while emptying a condemned unit

controls.control: Condemn on the spot. Pitted, bulged, fire-damaged, arc-struck or out of test means it never gets pressurised again — recover or discharge the contents by the right route for that agent, drill or stamp it out of service, and take it away so nobody puts it back on the bracket.
Do not hand-discharge a suspect unit to empty it. It goes to the discharge bay behind a barricade, or it is emptied through the recovery unit.

HFC (FM-200/HFC-227ea, HFC-125, HFC-236fa) and halon are recovered into a recovery cylinder on a recovery unit. They are not vented, not cracked off into the plant room, and not "let down slowly outside". Venting to atmosphere is only ever for CO2, nitrogen and inert blends. Record the recovered mass and the recovery cylinder number on the job card — that record is what proves the agent was not released.
Read the shoulder stamps before the gauge: manufacture date, last hydrostatic test date and test station number, and the stamped tare and fill mass. The stamps outrank the label.
A CO2 unit has no gauge — do not look for one. Weigh it against the stamped tare to know what is in it.
Service and record against AS 1851-2012 (Amd 1:2016) Section 10 for portables and Section 6 for special hazard systems; assess the cylinder itself against AS 2030.1:2026.
Glasses and gloves on before the first unit comes off the bracket.

steps.step: Isolate the gaseous suppression system before going near the cylinder bank
hazards: Unplanned agent discharge into an occupied room
Oxygen displacement — nitrogen, argon and inert blends give no warning and no smell
CO2 poisoning — CO2 makes you incapable well before it has displaced enough air to move an oxygen reading
Discharge noise causing hearing damage and disorientation
Door releases, damper drops and dumped air conditioning trapping you in the room
Shock or arc flash at the FIP or the releasing panel
Brigade turnout and a charged-out false alarm

controls.control: Releasing circuit to isolate at the FIP or the releasing panel. Your own lock and danger tag on the isolate switch; you keep the key in your pocket for the whole visit.
Cover and lock the local manual release station before you enter the protected space. Anyone can lean on one of those.

Fit the cylinder safety pin or locking cap, then remove the electric solenoid or pneumatic actuator from the cylinder valve. The actuator comes off before any other work on that cylinder — every time, no exception.
Panel door closed and latched every time you step away from it, even to walk to the truck. Nothing inside the panel's mains supply compartment is opened, touched or tested by you.
Ring the monitoring company and the building manager first. Get the isolation job number written on the job card before anything is switched.

Your work stops at the extra-low voltage releasing circuits and the field wiring. Work on the mains side, inside the supply compartment, or on any part of the installation that is electrical work is for a licensed electrician under the Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld), and work on or near energised electrical equipment is governed by Part 8 Division 3 of the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld). If the job needs the panel supply off, you book an electrician — you do not have a go.

Test before touch on any circuit you are treating as dead: prove the tester on a known live source, test the conductors, prove the tester again. A tester that has not been proved twice has told you nothing.

Run the room's mechanical ventilation the whole time you are inside, and hold the door open. If the door is a fire door or part of the room's gas-tight envelope, use a hold-open that releases on alarm — never a wedge, a toolbox or a fire extinguisher propped against it.

Wear the gas monitor matched to the agent in that bank while you are in the protected space: oxygen for nitrogen, argon and inert blends; a CO2 sensor or a multi-gas instrument with a CO2 channel where the agent is CO2. An oxygen monitor will not save you in a CO2 room. Walk out on the first alarm and do not silence it and keep working.
A second person is present or in continuous phone or radio contact for the whole time you are in the protected space, knows where you are and knows to call 000 rather than come in after you.
Sign the isolation into the site's impairment register and hang a sign on the door: system isolated, agent room, do not enter.

steps.responsible: Technician holding the special hazard fire system licence

steps.step: Enter a confined space where the cylinder bank sits in a pit, tank room or unventilated void
hazards: Oxygen-deficient or agent-contaminated atmosphere with no natural ventilation
Agent heavier than air pooling in the bottom of a pit, where you put your head last and your feet first
Single entry point, vertical access, and no way out under your own power once you are affected
Worker collapsing out of sight and out of earshot with nobody watching
The would-be rescuer becoming the second casualty
Plant or pipework feeding agent, water or fumes into the space while you are in it

controls.control: Do the work from outside the space. Most of it can be: isolate at the panel, read the stamps and the supervision from the hatch, and bring the cylinder out to open air on the trolley before you service it. Entry is the last resort, not the default, and "it's quicker" is not a reason to go in.

Everything that can feed the space is isolated and locked before anybody enters: the releasing circuit, the discharge manifold, and any pipework carrying agent, water or fuel through the space. Your lock, your tag, your key.
Forced ventilation with clean air into the space before entry and running for the whole entry. Never purge or ventilate with oxygen and never with a cylinder of anything else.
Retrieval harness and line on the entrant, anchored outside the space, wherever the access shape allows one to be used and hauled.

Confined space entry permit issued and signed before anybody's head goes below the lip. A plant room key, a site induction and a toolbox talk are not an entry permit. Sign every entry to the space, as s 68 of the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) requires.

Test the atmosphere from outside before entry — top, middle and bottom of the space, because the agent sits low — and monitor continuously while anyone is inside. Test for oxygen and for the agent that is in that bank. Get out on the first alarm.

A standby person stays outside the space for the whole entry, in continuous two-way communication with the entrant and watching the work where they can see it. The standby person does not wander off, does not take another job, and does not enter to rescue. That is what s 69 of the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) requires: continuous communication with the worker from outside the space, and monitoring of conditions by a standby person in the vicinity.

Written rescue plan agreed and rehearsed before the permit is signed, and it must get the entrant out without the standby person going in: haul on the retrieval line, or 000 with the location, the access route and the agent named. Whoever rings and whoever hauls is decided by name before entry, not worked out during it.
Harness where a retrieval line is used; gas monitor worn on the collar in the breathing zone, not clipped to the belt and not left sitting at the hatch.

steps.responsible: Technician holding the special hazard fire system licence, with a trained standby person

steps.step: Disconnect and remove a cylinder from the bank
hazards: Stored energy in the discharge manifold
Cylinder rocketing if the valve is knocked off — it will go through a block wall
Flexible discharge hose whipping when the union is cracked
Residual agent in the manifold blowing back
Dropping 50 to 100 kg onto feet or hands; pinch points in the bracket

controls.control: Anti-recoil cap or outlet plug goes onto the cylinder valve before the flexible discharge hose comes off. No cap, no disconnect.
Vent the manifold and confirm the manifold gauge reads zero before the union is cracked. Stand to the side of the union, not over it.
Cylinder stays strapped in its bracket until the hose is off and the cap is on. Strap the trolley to the cylinder before the bracket clamp is released — never the other way round.
Purpose-made cylinder trolley with a chain and a wheel brake, set on the brake before the transfer.

Two people or a mechanical aid on anything over 16 kg coming out of a rack or down out of an upper tier. That 16 kg trigger is the same everywhere in this statement — there is no second, higher number.

Look at the flexible discharge hose as it comes off: date stamp, ferrule corrosion, kinks, a hose that has whipped before. Tag a failed hose at the truck straight away so it cannot go back on at reinstall.
Steel cap boots, gloves and glasses; face shield if the manifold has not been proven at zero.

steps.step: Move 9 kg and 50 kg units by hand
hazards: Back, shoulder and knee strain from repeated lifting across a thirty-unit site
Crush to feet and fingers when a unit is set down
Stairs, ramps, kerbs and door thresholds with a loaded trolley
Awkward carries through a crowded plant room or a basement carpark

controls.control: Bring the tools to the unit. Most six-monthly work is done on the bracket without lifting the extinguisher off the wall at all.
Trolley or stair-climber, not arms. If it will not fit in the lift, it does not go down the stairs by hand — it waits for the goods lift or a second person.
A 50 kg cylinder is never carried. It is wheeled on a cylinder trolley with the chain across, and it is chocked whenever it is standing free.

Nothing over 16 kg lifted alone from floor level. Two people or a mechanical aid on anything above that, and agree the lift out loud before it starts: who takes the weight, where it lands, who calls it.

Break the run. Do not do thirty six-monthlies in one unbroken stretch of carrying — split it with the paperwork and the panel work. To be straight about it: the 16 kg trigger point is ours, not the law's. Neither s 60 of the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) nor the Hazardous manual tasks Code of Practice 2021 sets a safe maximum weight, and the Code says plainly that there isn't one. What s 60(2) does require is that we have regard to postures, movements, forces and vibration, to duration and frequency, to environmental conditions and to the design of the work area — which is why the run gets broken up as well as the weights capped.
Grip gloves and steel cap boots.

steps.step: Load and restrain in the vehicle
hazards: Cylinder rolling loose in the tray
Valve or actuator knocked off in a hard stop
Agent leak accumulating in an enclosed cabin or canopy
Lifting up into a high tray
Emergency services given the wrong description of the load

controls.control: Valve guards or caps back on, actuators removed and boxed separately from the cylinders they belong to. This does not make the cylinder safe — it is still full and still pressurised — it just puts something between the valve and the next pothole.
Nothing pressurised in the passenger cabin. Canopy vents open, tray unsealed.
Upright in the rack, ratchet-strapped to a rated anchor. A cylinder that cannot stand upright is laid down fore-and-aft, chocked so it cannot roll, and strapped.
Ramp or tailgate lift into the tray — nobody lifts a 50 kg cylinder to chest height.
Load and restrain to the National Transport Commission Load Restraint Guide.

Write the load down properly before you drive. Portable extinguishers travel as UN 1044, Class 2.2. A bulk suppression cylinder is NOT UN 1044 — it travels under the UN number of the gas inside it (for example carbon dioxide is UN 1013; nitrogen, argon, inert blends, HFC-227ea and HFC-125 each have their own). Take the proper shipping name and UN number for every cylinder off the cylinder label and the supplier's SDS, not off memory and not off this page, and write them on the transport document that stays in the cab. Count the load against the tools-of-trade limits in the Transport Operations (Road Use Management—Dangerous Goods) Regulation 2018 (Qld) before you load.

steps.step: Drive, then unload at the workshop or the next site
hazards: Heat build-up in a closed tray in a Queensland summer raising cylinder pressure
Agent leak while driving
Unloading from tray height
Load shift on a rough access road or a steep basement ramp

controls.control: The cabin stays a cabin. Nothing pressurised travels in it, and the bulkhead or window between the cabin and the tray stays shut.
Tray or canopy vents left open for the whole trip so any leak goes to atmosphere instead of building up in an enclosed space.
Unload down a ramp with the trolley. Nothing gets lifted down off the tray by hand.
Park in shade with the vents open. Cylinders never get left in a closed vehicle in the sun — not for a lunch break, not for a site meeting.
Re-check the straps after the first few kilometres and after any rough access.
If you smell agent or hear a hiss, pull over, get out, open the tray from upwind and let it ventilate before you go near it.
Emergency information and an SDS for every agent carried, in the cab, current, and matching what is actually on the truck today.

steps.step: Discharge test in the discharge bay
hazards: Noise over 110 dB
CO2 dry ice and cold burns to hands and face
CO2 poisoning at concentrations well below anything an oxygen meter will flag
Oxygen displacement in the bay or in any low point it drains into
Dry chemical dust cloud — respiratory irritation and total loss of visibility
Hose whip and the unit taking off if it is not held
Agent and propellant in the eyes
Fluorinated foam (PFAS) reaching ground, a stormwater grate or the sewer

controls.control: Do not discharge what is not due. AS 1851-2012 (Amd 1:2016) says which units come due for a discharge test and when; a unit that is not due does not get emptied to tidy up the paperwork or to use up an old charge.

Discharge outdoors or in the purpose-built bay — never in a plant room, a lift lobby, a basement or any room you cannot walk straight out of. Be clear about what the bay does: it does not remove the hazard, it puts a wall between the hazard and everybody else.
Unit clamped in the discharge bracket with the hose restrained before the pin comes out. Nobody holds a 50 kg unit while it discharges.
Bunded bay with extraction running; discharge downwind and clear of air intakes, windows and pedestrian routes.
Bund drain valve shut and checked shut before the pin comes out on any foam or wet chemical unit. Foam discharges into the bund and stays in the bund.

One person in the bay and one person outside it, and the person outside stays outside. They keep line of sight through the window or the camera and continuous two-way radio or phone contact for the whole discharge, and they do not walk in to help. Nobody discharges CO2 or an inert agent alone — not ever, not for one small unit, not because it is early and nobody else is in yet.

Gas detection matched to the agent, worn on the person in the bay and checked by the person outside: an oxygen monitor alarming at 19.5% oxygen for nitrogen, argon and inert blends; a CO2 sensor or a multi-gas instrument with a CO2 channel for any CO2 discharge. An oxygen monitor is the wrong instrument for CO2 — CO2 makes you incapable long before it has displaced enough air to pull oxygen down to 19.5%, so the alarm you are relying on sounds after you are already in trouble. CO2 alarm points are set at the bench to the current Safe Work Australia workplace exposure limits for carbon dioxide, the instrument is bump tested before the shift, and you leave on the first alarm.

Before any CO2 or inert-gas discharge: the bay's breathing apparatus set is checked, in date and staged outside the bay door, and the person outside is trained and fit tested in it. If nobody on the crew is BA-trained, the discharge still happens with the standby outside — but their job in an emergency is to call 000 and keep everyone out, and they must be told that before it starts, not afterwards.
Written rescue plan for the bay, agreed before the first pin comes out: who calls, from where, what they say, and how the room gets ventilated from outside. Nobody works it out through a closed door.

Foam concentrate and washdown water out of the bund goes into a labelled drum and off site with a licensed waste contractor, with the tracking paperwork kept on the job. Nothing fluorinated goes to ground, to the stormwater grate or down the sewer — not a rinse, not a hose-down, not "only a bit". That is a Queensland environmental offence as well as a PFAS release.
Sign on the bay door, and tell the site before an alarm or a discharge can be heard.
Class 5 hearing protection, face shield over glasses, cold-resistant gloves on CO2 horns, P2 for dry chemical.

steps.responsible: Technician in the bay, with a second person stationed outside it

steps.step: Internal inspection, valve removal and hydrostatic test
hazards: Residual pressure behind a valve that reads empty on the gauge
A CO2 cylinder with no gauge at all, assumed empty because it looks empty
A live expellant cartridge driving the head assembly off the shell
Valve firing out of the neck under stored pressure
Stripped or corroded neck threads letting go
Cylinder rupture on the hydrostatic rig
Dry chemical dust; wet chemical alkali burns
HFC or halon agent released while opening a shell

controls.control: GAUGED STORED-PRESSURE UNITS — prove zero twice: gauge at zero, then crack the valve to atmosphere and hear it. A gauge lies, the crack does not. The valve does not come out of the neck until it has been cracked.

CO2 UNITS — there is no gauge on a CO2 extinguisher or a CO2 suppression cylinder, so there is nothing to read and nothing to prove zero on. Weigh it against the stamped tare. Anything over tare still has agent in it, and until the scales say otherwise you treat it as full. It only comes apart after a full controlled discharge in the bay and a vent-down, clamped in the vice, with the valve broken out on the proper valve-removal tool from behind the barrier. Never a shifter, never a pipe wrench, never over your own body.

CARTRIDGE-OPERATED UNITS — the expellant cartridge comes out first and the shell is vented before the head assembly is loosened. A cartridge left in with a punctured seal will drive the head off the shell and into whatever is in front of it. Weigh the cartridge against its stamped mass: any loss and it is replaced, not refitted, and the allowable loss comes out of AS 1851-2012 (Amd 1:2016) Section 10 — look it up, do not guess it.
Cylinder clamped in the vice with the body pointing away from people and away from the door while the valve is broken out.
Hydrostatic testing inside a rated test jacket or enclosure with the controls outside it. A cylinder is never pressurised standing in the open workshop.

HFC and halon agent comes out into a recovery cylinder on the recovery unit before the shell is opened — never vented, never blown down to atmosphere to save time. Log the recovered mass and the recovery cylinder number.

Test, inspect and stamp to AS 2030.1:2026 and AS 2030.5:2026, at a certificated gas cylinder test station working to AS 2337.1-2004. Sight the station's own current certificate and its station number — do not accept "we work to AS 2337.1" as an answer. Stamp the shoulder with the station number and the date.
Failures get destroyed the same day — neck drilled or shell cut — not stacked in the corner where they can drift back into stock.
P2 and glasses for dry chemical; apron and gauntlets for wet chemical and foam.

steps.step: Refill and re-pressurise
hazards: Over-pressurisation and cylinder rupture
Under-charge, so the unit is signed off and will not throw agent when it is needed
Nitrogen charging line whipping if the coupling lets go
Wrong agent, or two agents mixed in one shell
Overfilling past the stamped fill mass
Nitrogen or inert gas building up in the fill room and displacing oxygen
CO2 building up in the fill room at concentrations an oxygen meter will not flag

controls.control: Regulator on the nitrogen charging line fitted with a relief valve set ABOVE the unit's stamped charging pressure and comfortably BELOW the cylinder's stamped test pressure — high enough that a normal fill never lifts it, low enough that it lifts long before the shell is in trouble. Check the set point and log it before the first fill of the day. If it lifts during a normal fill, the regulator is wrong or faulty and it gets fixed. It never gets wound up, packed out or bypassed to finish the job.
Charge behind a barricade or in a fill cage. Nobody stands over or in front of a unit while it is coming up to pressure.
Whip check or restraint on the charging hose coupling, on before the gas is turned on.
Mechanically ventilated fill room, running whenever anybody is filling — nitrogen, CO2 and inert blends give no warning at all.

Fill room detection matched to what is in the room: an oxygen monitor alarming at 19.5% oxygen where nitrogen, argon or inert blends are used; a CO2 sensor or a multi-gas instrument with a CO2 channel wherever CO2 is filled or decanted. An oxygen meter will not warn you about CO2 in time. CO2 alarm points are set at the bench to the current Safe Work Australia workplace exposure limits for carbon dioxide, the instrument is bump tested before the shift, and everybody leaves on the first alarm.
THE AGENT IS CHARGED BY MASS. Calibrated scales, in date, against the tare and fill mass stamped on the cylinder, to AS 2030.5:2026. Never by eye, never past the stamp.

THE EXPELLANT NITROGEN IS CHARGED BY PRESSURE. To the charging pressure stamped on the unit, at the reference temperature marked on it, corrected for the actual temperature of the cylinder — a unit charged while it is hot reads high on the gauge and ends up under-pressurised once it cools in the van. Gauge calibrated and in date. These are two different operations on the same unit: agent by mass, expellant by pressure. Do not run one rule over both.
Same agent back into the same shell. Check the agent against the label, the stamp and the register before the funnel goes in.

Only a person trained and signed off under the test station's own procedures fills a cylinder. Where the agent is an HFC or halon, that person also holds the Commonwealth extinguishing agent handling licence.
Face shield, P2 and gloves for the whole fill and charge.

steps.step: Reinstall, restore the system and hand it back
hazards: System left isolated overnight and nobody knows
Actuator left off, or the safety pin left in, so the system will not fire
Cylinder left unstrapped in the bracket
A time-expired or damaged flexible discharge hose refitted and left to fail at full system pressure
False discharge the moment the releasing circuit is re-energised
Unannounced brigade turnout

controls.control: Your lock and danger tag stay on the isolate switch until every item on the walk-through has been ticked off in front of you. The lock comes off last, it comes off by your hand, and nobody else cuts it.

Reconnect in this order and do not vary it: cylinder into the bracket and strapped, then the anti-recoil cap or outlet plug off, then the discharge hose on and tight, then the actuator on, then the safety pin out — last thing you touch. The cap sits on the same outlet the hose screws onto, so it has to come off immediately before the hose goes on. Have the hose and the spanner in your hand first; a capless, unconnected cylinder does not stand in the bracket while you go looking for a tool.

Check the flexible discharge hose before it goes back on: date stamp in date, no kinks, no corrosion at the ferrule, no sign it has whipped. Out of date or damaged means it is replaced, not refitted. If you have not got a replacement on the truck, the cylinder stays out and the system stays isolated in writing — you do not fit a doubtful hose to close the job.
Confirm at the panel that the cylinder pressure switch or weight supervision reads normal, and that no fault or isolate remains on the display, before the isolate comes off.

Two-person walk-through against the isolation tag: every pin, every cap, every strap, every manual release cover, every actuator. One reads the list out, the other puts a hand on the item. Not one person doing both.
Ring the monitoring company back, restore the circuit, get the confirmation number, write it on the job card before you leave the site.

Tag and record every unit to AS 1851-2012 (Amd 1:2016) Section 10 and Section 6: work done, next test date, defects found and defects left. Record any agent recovered and where it went. Sign the record and give the occupier their copy — that record is what the Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) requires the owner to hold.

If the system is not going back into service today, that goes to the building manager in writing before you drive off, with the date it will be restored and who is coming back. A verbal "I'll be back Tuesday" to whoever is at the front desk is not a handover.

emergency:
UNCONTROLLED AGENT RELEASE (plant room, discharge bay or fill room): get out, pull the door shut behind you, leave the tools. Raise the alarm, account for everyone at the site assembly area. Nobody goes back in until the room has been mechanically ventilated and the atmosphere is verified safe on a calibrated instrument that reads the agent that was released — oxygen for nitrogen, argon and inert blends; CO2 on a CO2 channel where CO2 was released. An oxygen reading above 19.5% does NOT prove a room is safe after a CO2 release. Call 000.

PERSON DOWN IN A PLANT ROOM, PIT, DISCHARGE BAY OR FILL ROOM: do not go in. Going in after them is how the second person dies. Call 000, say the agent by name, say the atmosphere may be oxygen-deficient or CO2-loaded, and say whether the person is in a confined space. Get the room's ventilation running from outside if you can reach the switch from outside. If there is a retrieval line on them, haul from outside. Only a person trained and fit tested in breathing apparatus, wearing it, with someone else outside, goes through that door before the brigade arrives.

CYLINDER ROCKETING OR VALVE FAILURE: clear the area and keep everyone back behind cover. Call 000 and tell the operator there are pressurised cylinders. Do not approach a cylinder that has been in a fire, even after the fire is out — it can still BLEVE.

VEHICLE FIRE WITH CYLINDERS ON BOARD: stop, get out, move at least 100 m upwind and keep others back. Call 000 and tell them exactly what is on the vehicle, read off the transport document and the cylinder labels in the cab — the proper shipping name and UN number of every cylinder, not a general description. Do not say "fire extinguishers" if you have suppression cylinders on board: UN 1044 covers portable extinguishers only, and a crew told UN 1044 will size up the wrong hazard for a ute carrying bulk CO2, nitrogen, inert blend or HFC cylinders.

CO2 COLD BURN: flush with lukewarm running water, do not rub, do not use hot water, do not peel clothing off frozen skin. Medical assessment same day.

DRY CHEMICAL OR WET CHEMICAL IN THE EYES: irrigate at the eyewash for 15 minutes, holding the lid open. Wet chemical is a potassium salt and alkaline — keep flushing and go to hospital, do not stop early because it feels better.

CRUSH FROM A DROPPED CYLINDER: do not roll or lift the cylinder off a trapped limb without support and a second person. First aid, 000, and support the limb where it lies.

FOAM OR AGENT ESCAPING TO GROUND, A STORMWATER GRATE OR A DRAIN: stop the source, dam it and contain it with whatever is on the truck — spill socks, sand, a shovelled bund. Do not hose it away. Ring the office immediately: a fluorinated foam release to stormwater or sewer is a reportable environmental incident, not a clean-up you sort out quietly.

SUSPECTED BACK OR SHOULDER STRAIN: stop for the day, do not finish the run to be helpful. Report it before you go home.

Emergency 000. Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26. Ring the office immediately. Any notifiable incident under s 38 of the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) is reported to Workplace Health and Safety Queensland on 1300 362 128, and the site is not disturbed until they say so — except to help an injured person or make it safe.
references: Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) — primary duty of care (s 19); duty to notify a notifiable incident (s 38); duty to consult workers (ss 47-48)

Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 60 — managing risks to health and safety from a musculoskeletal disorder associated with a hazardous manual task; s 60(2) lists the matters to have regard to, including postures, movements, forces and vibration (a), duration and frequency (b), workplace environmental conditions (c), design of the work area (d)

Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) ss 68-69 — confined spaces: signage at every entry, continuous communication with the worker from outside the space, and monitoring of conditions by a standby person in the vicinity of the space

Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 289 — meaning of construction work; s 289(1) includes decommissioning, s 289(2)(e) includes the installation, testing or maintenance of an essential service in relation to a structure, s 289(3)(d) excludes testing, maintenance or repair work of a minor nature

siteSpecificPrompts: Is today's work minor testing and maintenance, or is it decommissioning, cylinder removal or an extended isolation — and if it is the latter, which s 291 category applies and who has been told this is HRCW?
Which suppression system is in this room, what agent, and how many cylinders in the bank?

Is the agent an HFC (FM-200/HFC-227ea, HFC-125, HFC-236fa) or halon — and if so, who on the crew holds the extinguishing agent handling licence, and is the recovery unit and an empty recovery cylinder on the truck?
Where is the releasing panel, and who holds the key to the isolate switch?
Who is the monitoring company, and what is today's isolation job number?
Who is the building manager or fire safety adviser, and have they signed the impairment off?
Where is the local manual release, and has it been covered and locked before you entered the protected space?

Does this plant room have mechanical ventilation, does it keep running with the door shut, and is the door a fire door or part of a gas-tight envelope (so the hold-open must be one that releases on alarm)?
Which gas instrument does this agent need — oxygen, or a CO2 channel? Is it bump tested today and is the calibration sticker in date?

Could this space meet the definition of a confined space under AS/NZS 2865:2009 (Amd 1:2025) — and if so, where is the entry permit, who is the standby person, and what is the rescue plan that does not put them inside?
What is the heaviest unit on this site, and can it be wheeled the whole way, or are there stairs, kerbs or a lift that is too small?
Where can the vehicle park so no cylinder is carried more than a few metres?
Where is the nearest safe discharge point, and is it clear of air intakes, windows, walkways and the carpark?
Are any foam units being discharge tested today — where does the bund drain go, and who is taking the collected foam and washdown water away?
Who else is working in this plant room today, and do they know the system is isolated?
Where is the assembly area, the closest first aid kit, the closest eyewash and the closest defibrillator?
Is the building occupied, and who has to be told before any alarm can sound or any agent can discharge?
Is the system going back into service today, or does it stay isolated overnight — and who has been told in writing if it does?
