title: Working at Height — Ladders, EWPs and Roofs
activity: Reaching detectors, sprinkler heads, valves, tank tops and hydrant boosters from platform ladders, elevating work platforms and roofs.

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(a)
hrcw.text: involves a risk of a person falling more than 2m

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(d)
hrcw.text: involves, or is likely to involve, the disturbance of asbestos

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(f)
hrcw.text: is carried out in or near a confined space

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(k)
hrcw.text: is carried out on or near energised electrical installations or services

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(n)
hrcw.text: is carried out on, in or adjacent to a road, railway, shipping lane or other traffic corridor that is in use by traffic other than pedestrians

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(o)
hrcw.text: is carried out in an area at a workplace in which there is any movement of powered mobile plant

whenRequired:
Any time your feet leave the floor to reach a device. Signed before the first ladder goes up, not written up afterwards. It covers a platform ladder in a corridor, a mobile scaffold in a plant room or corridor, a scissor or boom in a warehouse or carpark, and any trip onto a roof, gantry or tank top.

WHY IT IS HIGH RISK CONSTRUCTION WORK. Section 289(2)(e) of the Regulation says the installation, testing or maintenance of an essential service in relation to a structure is construction work, so AS 1851 routine service at height is construction work — Safe QLD does not argue the "work of a minor nature" exclusion at s 289(3)(d) in front of an inspector. Six paragraphs of s 291 can bite on this job: (a) a fall of more than 2m, (o) an area with any movement of powered mobile plant, (k) work on or near energised electrical installations or services (ceiling voids, lighting circuits, the FIP and switchboards), and (n) work on or adjacent to a traffic corridor in use by traffic other than pedestrians (carparks, loading docks, live vehicle lanes). Two more are conditional and are STOP-AND-ESCALATE triggers, not things this statement controls: (d) disturbance of asbestos — the moment fibre cement sheeting is likely to be disturbed, stop and ring the supervisor; and (f) work in or near a confined space — which flags tank-top work next to an open or openable hatch. Entry into a tank, plenum or riser is NOT covered here: that is a confined space, get the entry permit and the confined space statement.

NOBODY WEARS A HARNESS ALONE, AND NOBODY GOES ON A ROOF ALONE. Section 306I(13) says a person conducting a business or undertaking must not use, or allow another person to use, a fall arrest harness system while the person using it is alone. It is penalty-backed. Company rule on top of it: no solo roof access at all, whatever system is worn, because the rescue step does not work without a second person. If the second person cannot be there, the job does not proceed and is rebooked.

UNDER 2m IS NOT NOTHING. The 2m line decides whether the work is high risk construction work, not whether it is a hazard. Section 78 applies to any fall from one level to another that is reasonably likely to cause injury, and s 306C applies to construction work with a fall of less than 2m (though not to a fall from a ladder — s 306C(2)(a) — which is covered instead by ss 306K to 306M). A 1.8m drop onto a concrete plant room floor, a bench edge or an open riser door is still a controlled risk.

IF THE JOB STOPS MATCHING THIS STATEMENT — different access, a different machine, a hazard not listed here, a control you cannot actually apply — stop the work, ring the supervisor, and do not restart until the statement has been changed to match. Section 300(2) requires exactly that: work not carried out in accordance with the SWMS must be stopped immediately or as soon as it is safe to do so, and resumed only in accordance with the statement. Changing the method on the fly without changing the statement is a breach on its own.

A STEP RATED HIGH RESIDUAL DOES NOT START ON THE TECHNICIAN'S SIGN-ON ALONE. It needs the supervisor's sign-off on the day, naming at least one additional control, or the job is rebooked with different access.

CONSULTATION. Record on the sign-on sheet who was consulted in preparing and reviewing this statement, and consult the crew again on site before work starts — WHS Act ss 47 to 49 require the workers who will do the work to be consulted when hazards are identified and when decisions are made about controlling them, and it is the first thing an inspector asks about a SWMS. Review and revise the statement whenever s 38 of the Regulation is triggered (a control not working, a change at the workplace, a new hazard, consultation indicating a review, or a health and safety representative asking) — s 302.

OUT OF SCOPE: confined space entry; erecting, altering or dismantling a scaffold from which a person or object could fall more than 4m (that is licensed scaffolding work and needs a scaffolder and a separate statement); hot work; and any electrical work within the meaning of the Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld).
permits: Roof access permit or hatch key from the building manager, booked before the day
Site working-at-height permit where the site issues one (shopping centres, hospitals, schools, ports)
FIP isolation and impairment notice before any detector or sprinkler head is disturbed
Sprinkler stop valve lock-out and drain-down authority from the building's fire safety adviser

Written interim protection agreement before the system is impaired — who does the fire watch, over what area, at what patrol interval, and the agreed maximum impairment duration recorded on the impairment notice
Confined space entry permit — required if a tank, plenum or riser is entered, and outside this SWMS
Hot work permit where any cutting, grinding or brazing is done at height, with the hot work SWMS
Electrical isolation by a licensed electrical worker, proved de-energised and locked out, before any work on or beside a lighting or mains circuit at ceiling level
Supply authority permit, isolation or line covering where the EWP cannot stay outside the exclusion zone for an overhead electric line under the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld)
ppe: Hard hat with chin strap (a helmet without one leaves the platform before you do)
Safety glasses — ceiling dust and rust scale come straight down when a head is unscrewed
Hi-vis long sleeve shirt, mandatory in any warehouse or carpark with plant movement
Lace-up safety boots with slip-resistant sole, done up before you climb

Full body harness to AS/NZS 1891.1:2020 (Personal equipment for work at height, Part 1: Manufacturing requirements for full body combination and lower body harnesses), in date, with the six-monthly inspection tag legible
Lanyard or adjustable restraint line sized so it cannot reach the edge, with double-action (twin-action) connectors at both ends — "double action" describes the hook, not the lanyard
Tool lanyards on every tool and torch taken above ground level
Closed tool pouch for detector heads, screws and glass bulbs — not shirt pockets
Cut-resistant gloves for rusted roof deck, purlins, sprinkler pipework and ceiling grid
P2 disposable respirator for dusty or contaminated ceiling and roof spaces (insulation, bird and rodent droppings), fit-checked before you go up
Long sleeves, broad brim under the helmet and sunscreen for roof work
training: General construction induction card (white card) — s 316 puts the duty to PROVIDE the training on the business; s 317(1) is the one that bites in the field: do not direct or allow a worker to carry out construction work unless they have completed the training and, if they completed it more than 2 years ago, have carried out construction work in the preceding 2 years; s 317(2) requires them to hold the card (or a certification issued within the preceding 60 days)
Working at heights competency covering harness fitting, anchor selection and rescue (RIIWHS204 or equivalent), refreshed on the company cycle
WP high risk work licence for a boom-type elevating work platform where the length of the boom is 11m or more (schedule 3, item 21; TLILIC0005)
Scissor lift and under-11m boom: EWPA operator card and machine-specific familiarisation on the actual model before it leaves the yard
Ground crew trained on the ground controls and emergency lowering of the machine in use
Rescue-from-height competency for at least one person on site whenever a harness is worn — and the rescue procedure itself tested under s 80(3), not just read
Current first aid and CPR on the crew
QBCC fire protection occupational licence for the fire work being carried out at height

Licensing boundary, known by every technician: a QBCC fire protection licence does NOT authorise electrical work. Electrical work is defined in s 18 of the Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld) and s 55 of that Act requires an electrical work licence to perform or supervise it. Connecting or disconnecting the 240V supply to a FIP, and installing, testing, replacing, repairing or maintaining a mains-connected sounder, strobe or lighting circuit, is electrical work — book a licensed electrical worker

Asbestos awareness — and where a technician may carry out asbestos-related work, training in the identification and safe handling of, and control measures for, asbestos and ACM under s 445, with the record kept

steps.step: Plan the access before the day, from the office
hazards: Work scoped for a ladder that actually needs an EWP, so the technician improvises on site
Job scoped for one technician when the access chosen needs a harness, or needs a roof trip, and therefore needs two
Roof access not arranged, no key, no hatch code
Anchor points on the roof never certified or tag expired
Fragile or asbestos-containing roof sheeting nobody warned you about

controls.control: Reach it from the ground where you can. A telescopic smoke/heat test pole, a remote test point at the FIP, or a floor-level test valve means nobody goes up at all.

Where a device is over 2m and a machine can get to it, book the scissor or boom instead of a ladder. For a run of devices down a corridor or a plant room, book a mobile scaffold rather than repeatedly repositioning a ladder. Cost of the hire is not a reason to put a ladder up.

Crew the job for the access. If any part of it needs a harness, or needs anyone on a roof, it is a two-person job — s 306I(13) prohibits use of a fall arrest harness system while the person using it is alone, and the rescue step does not work without a second person. Put both names on the job before it is dispatched. If the second person cannot be there, reschedule; do not send one technician and hope.

Ring the site the day before: roof access route, who holds the key, hatch location, and the date on the anchor point inspection or certification tag. The Regulation requires a competent person to inspect harness-based systems at least every 6 months and to give a written record — s 306G(4) for travel restraint, s 306I(10)(c) for a fall arrest harness system. If nobody can produce a record, the anchor is not used.

Read the site's asbestos register before setting foot on any fibre cement roof. The person with management or control of the workplace must have one and must make it readily accessible to you (ss 425, 427). The register duty applies to buildings whenever constructed; the only carve-out is s 425(6) — a building constructed after 31 December 1989 where no asbestos has been identified and none is likely to be present. As a field rule, treat any fibre cement sheet installed before 2004 as ACM until the register says otherwise. If there is no register and the sheeting could be ACM, do not go on the roof — that is an s 291(d) trigger and it goes back to the supervisor.

Fill in the s 299(4) record on this job sheet — it is a mandatory field, not a suggestion. Where the only controls for a fall over 2m will be administrative or PPE (and a harness, restraint or arrest, is PPE), the SWMS must describe ALL control measures considered, addressing the s 79(3) ranking. Work down the ranking in writing and say why each was rejected: (1) fall prevention device — edge protection, guardrail, working platform, fall protection cover; (2) work positioning system — the tier this trade routinely skips, and often the right answer on a tank top or valve platform; (3) fall arrest, so far as is reasonably practicable. The note to s 79(3) says a combination may be used where one control alone is not enough.

steps.step: Sign in and walk the area before anything goes up
hazards: Forklifts, pallet jacks and delivery trucks moving through the aisle you are about to occupy
Public, staff or parked cars directly under the work
Suspended basement slab of unknown load capacity under a 2,500kg scissor or 6,000kg boom
Overhead electric lines, solar arrays and unfused mains across the yard or carpark
Pits, grates, service covers, speed humps and oil on the drive path

controls.control: Where the public, patients, students or shoppers can reach the drop zone, tape is not enough. Use hard barriers, a closed and signed door, or a person stationed at each entry, for the whole time the basket is up. In a live centre or hospital that person turns people back and does nothing else.

Keep the machine, the boom, your body and anything you are handling outside the exclusion zone for every overhead electric line. The distances are in schedule 2 of the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) — the 2013 regulation is repealed and the 2026 regulation commenced on 1 September 2026. For OPERATING PLANT such as an EWP operated by an untrained person, uninsulated line: 3m for low voltage and everything up to 132kV; 6m above 132kV up to 330kV; 8m above 330kV. On foot as an untrained person: 3m off any line you have not had consultation about, and 3m up to 132kV. If you cannot identify the voltage, treat it as unknown, assume the largest zone and ring the supply authority. Where the geometry does not allow clearance, the line is isolated or covered by the supply authority BEFORE the machine moves — not after you have had a go at it.

Cone and tape the drop zone before the machine goes up — at least the working height plus 2m out, with an OVERHEAD WORK — DO NOT ENTER sign at every entry to it. Understand what this is: a warning, not a barrier. Tape stops people who are paying attention.
Ask the warehouse or centre supervisor to stop forklift and truck movement through the aisle in writing, or move the work to out of hours. A verbal 'they'll go around you' is not a control.

Basement and suspended slabs: get written confirmation of the slab loading from the building manager before driving the EWP onto it. If nobody can produce it, the machine stays on grade and you find another way to the device.
Walk the drive path on foot first and mark the pits, grates and soft edges with cones before the machine moves.

steps.step: Isolate the system before you climb to it
hazards: Unwanted brigade attendance from a detector disturbed at ceiling level
Sprinkler head knocked at the ceiling, discharging over stock and people
Charged sprinkler line opened at a valve that reads shut but is not
Water on the floor below turning the ladder base or the EWP wheels into a slip
The building left unprotected while the zone is off line and the sprinklers are drained, with nobody watching it

controls.control: Isolate the affected zone or loop at the FIP and record it on the panel and in the site log book before any detector is removed or disturbed. Name the panel and the zone number in the log, not 'system isolated'.
For work on or near a head or valve: close and padlock the relevant sprinkler stop valve, drain down, and confirm zero pressure at the test and drain valve before touching anything at the ceiling.

INTERIM PROTECTION, agreed in writing with the building's fire safety adviser BEFORE anything is isolated: who is doing the fire watch, over what area, at what patrol interval, and what they do if they find smoke. Record the agreed maximum impairment duration on the impairment notice. If the impairment will run past that duration, or past close of business, stop and escalate to the supervisor and the occupier before it does — do not let it drift.

Ring the monitoring company and take the brigade connection off line before any test that can transmit, and ring it back on before you leave site. Impairment notice on the FIP for the duration, with your name and mobile on it.
Tag the isolation with your name and time, and set a phone alarm to restore it. Isolations left in overnight are how buildings burn.
Notify the building's fire safety adviser and, where the impairment is significant or extended, the occupier in writing before starting.
Mop or squeegee any water that reaches the floor before a ladder foot or a machine wheel goes near it, and cone the wet area. Draining down puts water where you are about to stand.

steps.step: Platform ladder and mobile scaffold work in corridors, plant rooms and ceiling spaces
hazards: Overreaching sideways to a detector and taking the ladder over
Ladder kicked out by a passing trolley or a door swung open into it
Fall onto hard floor, edge of a bench, or open riser door
Metal stiles brought into contact with a lighting circuit while working at the ceiling
Falling through a suspended ceiling — tiles, plasterboard, grid and battens carry no person
Stepping off the ladder onto ceiling battens or grid to reach the next device
Unprotected, damaged or unidentified live wiring and open junction boxes in the ceiling void
Sharp ceiling grid, screws and fixings at head and hand height
Fibreglass and mineral wool insulation, and accumulated bird and rodent droppings, disturbed dry
Severe heat load in a Queensland roof space in the afternoon
Mobile scaffold moved with a person or tools still on the deck

controls.control: Use a platform ladder or step platform with a guardrailed top, not a stepladder. It gives you both hands and something around you at the working level.

For a run of devices down a ceiling line, use a mobile scaffold rather than repositioning a ladder twenty times. Rules for it: fully decked; guardrails and toe boards fitted; castors locked before anyone climbs; nobody and nothing on the deck while it is moved; no ladder, drum or box on the deck to gain height; scaffold tag current and filled in. If the platform is high enough that a person or object could fall more than 4m, erecting, altering or dismantling it is licensed scaffolding work — stop, and get a licensed scaffolder. Safe QLD technicians use a mobile scaffold, they do not build one over 4m.

Barricade the corridor both sides and wedge or lock any door that opens into the ladder. In a school, hospital or aged care corridor a second person stands and turns people back — tape alone will not hold.

Where you must work on or beside a lighting or mains circuit at ceiling level, it is isolated by a licensed electrical worker, locked out, and PROVED de-energised with a tester at the point of work before you start. Do not rely on the switch. This mirrors what the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) requires for electrical work on or near energised equipment: the equipment is tested by a competent person to decide whether it is energised, and every exposed part is treated as energised until it is isolated and found not to be.

Ladder rated at least 120kg and marked for industrial use — s 306M(1)(a) and (b) make both a duty, not a preference, and s 306M(1)(c) and (d) say it is used only for what it was designed for and not loaded beyond its rating. Fibreglass stiles for anything near lighting circuits, the FIP or a switchboard.

Never use a ladder to support a platform or a plank. Ladder platform brackets and planks spanning two ladders are prohibited for construction work in Queensland — s 306M(7): the person must not use, or allow another person to use, the ladder to support a platform. If you need to move along a ceiling line, move the platform ladder or get the mobile scaffold or the EWP.

Where you genuinely have to bear weight in a ceiling or roof space, work off a crawl board or platform that bears on structural members — trusses, joists, purlins — laid before you commit your weight, not after.

Ladder length limits, s 306M(1)(e): a single ladder no longer than 6.1m; an extension ladder no longer than 7.5m; an extension ladder used to do electrical work within the meaning of the Electrical Safety Act 2002 no longer than 9.2m. Above that the ladder is the wrong tool — get the scaffold or the machine.

The law: the bottom of the ladder on a stable surface and the rungs approximately level (s 306M(6)). Company rule on top of it: a dry surface, spreaders locked, not on a pallet, not on carpet over a floor waste, not bridging a step, not on a wet drain-down puddle.

Trunk stays inside the stiles at all times. Never stand higher than the second tread below the top plate of a stepladder, and never on the top plate. Move the ladder rather than reach for the next detector.

A single or extension ladder is only for access, or for 'permitted work' as s 306A defines it — the gear you carry does not restrict your movement or unbalance you, your trunk stays approximately centred between the stiles, and anything you use can be worked one-handed. Set it at 70° to 80° to the horizontal, and where it is a temporary means of access to or from a surface run it at least 1m above that surface (s 306M(8)). Where you will do permitted work from it and could fall 2m or more, it must ALSO be secured at or near the top or at or near the bottom to stop it moving (s 306L(3)(b)) — a second person footing it counts, and s 306L(3)(a) then requires 3 limbs on the ladder, or a pole strap, or a fall arrest harness system not attached to the ladder. Section 306L(4) lets you hold a stable object — guttering, a fixed plate — instead of the ladder itself.

A SUSPENDED CEILING CARRIES NO LOAD. Never step, kneel, lean or put a knee on ceiling tiles, grid, battens or plasterboard. Stay on the ladder platform or the scaffold deck, or work off a crawl board on structural members. If you cannot reach the device without leaving the platform, the platform is in the wrong place — get down and move it.

Treat every cable, junction box and fitting in a ceiling void as live until it is proved otherwise. Do not part, cut, move, re-clip or 'tidy' wiring that is not yours. A QBCC fire protection licence does not authorise electrical work: connecting or disconnecting the 240V supply to a FIP, and installing, testing, replacing, repairing or maintaining a mains-connected sounder, strobe or lighting circuit, is electrical work under s 18 of the Electrical Safety Act 2002 and needs an electrical work licence under s 55 of that Act. If the job needs it, stop and book a licensed electrical worker.

In a house, apartment building or private garage (Building Code of Australia class 1, 2 or 10a), the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) roof space provisions require the building's relevant electrical installation to be de-energised before a worker enters the roof space, unless that is not reasonably practicable or you are there to test, service or commission an energised non-electrical thing — and then a recorded risk assessment and a written statement of hazards and controls must be done first. Commercial buildings sit outside that division; the wiring in them is no safer, so apply the same discipline.

Check the void before you commit. A Queensland roof space in the afternoon will be well over 50°C — do ceiling work early, open hatches and ventilate first, work in short stints with a mate at the hatch, and come down before you get heat affected. Water in the ute is not water in the ceiling: take a bottle up.

P2 mask, gloves and long sleeves in any dusty or contaminated ceiling space. Do not disturb insulation or accumulated bird or rodent droppings dry — damp them down first, bag what you disturb, and wash your hands and face before you eat or touch your phone.

steps.step: Set up and pre-start the EWP
hazards: Overturn on soft ground, a drain, a pit lid or an unseen slope
Machine faults — flat battery on emergency lowering, seized gate latch, tilt alarm bypassed, elevated-travel interlock defeated
Log book out of date: annual service or ten-yearly major inspection overdue
Crush points at the scissor pack and the boom pivot during setup
An indoor-rated machine taken outside onto a dock, a carpark deck or an exposed roof area
A summer storm or lightning arriving while the basket is up

controls.control: Set on solid level ground within the machine's slope limit, outriggers on pads, and clear of pits, grates, drains, service covers and soft shoulders. Rough terrain only on a machine rated for it.
In a scissor lift the closed gate and guardrails are the fall protection. No harness unless the manufacturer's plate calls for one, and never climb or stand on the rails to gain height.

The elevated-travel interlock and the tilt cut-out are working and have not been bypassed — checked at pre-start, on the machine, not assumed. A machine with a defeated interlock or a bridged tilt alarm goes back on the truck and the hire company is told why.

Fill in the pre-start before use, on paper: emergency lowering tested FROM THE GROUND, controls, tyres and pins, chassis tilt alarm, gate latch and guardrails, and the log book in date for annual service and ten-yearly major inspection. A machine that fails the pre-start goes back on the truck.

Read the machine's plate for its wind rating and whether it is rated for outdoor use. An indoor-only machine — most electric scissors are — does not go outside, on a loading dock, or on an open carpark deck, at any wind speed, however short the job. Outdoors, stop work and lower fully when the wind exceeds the machine's rated limit; if you have no way to measure it, if it is moving the boom or you are bracing against it, it is too much.
Lower the machine fully and get off the roof at the first sign of an approaching storm or lightning, regardless of how much work is left. Come back tomorrow.

Hands, feet and cables clear of the scissor pack and the boom pivot while the machine is moving. Nobody stands in the pinch points to guide it, nobody reaches into the pack to free a lead or a strop, and the machine is fully lowered and the key out before anyone works around the pack.
A second person stays on the ground for the duration, trained on that machine's ground controls and emergency lowering, and in sight or radio contact. They are not doing paperwork in the ute.

In a boom lift, travel tower or cherry picker, wear the full body harness with the shortest lanyard that lets you work, clipped to the manufacturer's anchor point in the basket — never the handrail. Be clear what this is: restraint against being catapulted out, not fall arrest, and it is PPE — the bottom of the s 79(3) ranking, not an isolation control. The gate, the rails and where you put the basket are what actually keep you in.

steps.step: Work from the EWP at the detector, head or valve
hazards: Crushing between the basket rail and overhead pipework, racking, ducting or a beam — the way most EWP fatalities happen
Basket lurching when the boom is driven elevated or hits a floor joint
Contact with racking, roller doors or sprinkler pipe, dislodging stock or a head
Tools and detector heads dropped onto people and cars below
Technician stepping out of the basket at height onto a roof, gantry, plant deck, mezzanine or tank top to reach a device
Handling a heavy or awkward part, or a long test pole, over the basket rail

controls.control: Nobody in the drop zone while the basket is up. Hard barrier or a person at each entry where the public, staff or forklifts can reach it; cones and tape only where the area is genuinely closed.
Secondary guarding — anti-entrapment bar or pressure-sensing plate — stays fitted and working. Never fold it out of the way to get closer to a head.

DO NOT CLIMB INTO OR OUT OF THE BASKET WHILE IT IS ELEVATED. Enter and exit at ground level or on the chassis only. You do not step onto a roof, gantry, plant deck, mezzanine or tank top from the basket. The only exception is a machine specifically designed for transfer at height where the manufacturer's information permits it, and then only under a documented risk assessment, with a fall arrest system anchored to the STRUCTURE and connected before the gate opens, and with the transfer point named on the permit. If you are looking at a roof with no compliant access and an EWP already on site, that is not the answer — stop and ring the supervisor.
Look up before every movement, move in short bursts on one axis at a time, and stop the machine before you look away from the controls.
Approach the head or detector from beside it, never from directly beneath, so the basket cannot pin your chest against the pipe. Position first, then work.

Travel elevated only where the machine permits it, at creep speed, on flat clear ground. Otherwise lower fully, drive, and re-elevate. This is a driving rule that depends on you; the interlock checked at pre-start is what backs it up.
A spotter on the ground watches the boom and the overheads, not the technician working. Their job is the gap between the basket and the structure.

Nothing heavy or awkward is handed across the basket rail at height. Load valves, drums, spare heads and long parts into the basket at ground level, or hoist them on a rope. Keep the telescopic test pole as short as the ceiling allows, brace it on the rail rather than holding it out at arm's length, and swap operators before your shoulders give out.

steps.step: Get onto the roof
hazards: Fall from the access ladder while carrying gear
Fall through the open hatch after you are up
Cage ladder that funnels a fall rather than stopping it
Wet, mossy or dew-covered access at the top
Locked or seized hatch leaving you stranded on the ladder
Technician sent to the roof on their own

controls.control: Use the building's compliant fixed stair, fixed ladder and walkway to AS 1657:2018 where one exists. Do not lean a portable ladder against a parapet when a stair is available.

On a steep fixed ladder, clip to the ladder-mounted anchorage line or rail at the BASE before you leave the ground, locking device on the front attachment point, and the shortest lanyard the system takes so a slip is caught immediately rather than after a metre.

Close and latch the hatch behind you, or fit a fall protection cover or barricade over it. A fall protection cover has to be able to withstand the impact of a person falling onto it, and be securely fixed in place to prevent it being moved or removed accidentally — s 306F. A sheet of ply resting over the hole is not one.

NOBODY GOES ONTO A ROOF ALONE. Two people on any roof trip. Where a harness is worn it is not just company policy: s 306I(13) prohibits a business from using, or allowing another person to use, a fall arrest harness system while the person using it is alone. If the second person cannot be there, the job does not proceed and is rebooked.

An EWP is not a means of access onto a roof under this statement. If the only compliant access is missing, seized or locked and nobody can produce a key, that is a defect to report and a job to reschedule — not a reason to fly yourself up in the basket and step off.

Climbing a single or extension ladder to gain access: at least 2 hands and 1 foot, or 2 feet and 1 hand, on the ladder from when you are fully on it to when you are leaving it — s 306K(2)(a). The same rule is company practice on a fixed building ladder, which s 306K does not reach. Nothing in your hands, either direction.
Hoist tools and parts up on a rope in a closed bucket, or wear a backpack. Never climb with a toolbox or a detector under your arm. This is a work method and it only works if you do it every time.

Before you climb: key in your hand, hatch confirmed unlocked and free, and the top of the ladder checked for dew, moss or algae. Wet or mossy access means wait for it to dry or come back — there is nothing above worth a fall from the top of a cage ladder.

steps.step: Work on the roof — edges, skylights and fragile sheeting
hazards: Fall through fibre cement sheeting, rusted metal deck, or a polycarbonate roof light that looks solid from above
Fall from an unprotected edge, parapet, or the gap behind a plant deck
Slip on a wet, mossy or steeply pitched roof
Asbestos fibre release from cutting, drilling or standing on old fibre cement
Heat stress on a metal deck in a Queensland summer
Carrying valves, drums, spare heads or a test pole across an unprotected roof

controls.control: Do not go near the edge or the skylight. If the valve, gauge or device can be reached from the walkway, that is where you work — and if it cannot, that is a defect to raise, not a reason to walk the roof.

Where the roof has a compliant guardrail or walkway to AS 1657:2018, stay inside it. What compliant edge protection looks like under s 306E: a top rail at least 900mm above the base surface where that surface is at least 1,200mm wide (s 306E(4)(a)(i)) — measured differently, per s 306E(4)(a)(ii), where it is narrower or sloped; a bottom rail 150mm to 250mm up, or a toe board at least 150mm high fitted below all rails (s 306E(5)(a)); no gap over 450mm between any rail and its nearest rail or the toe board (s 306E(5)(b)); and on a roof pitched over 26°, sturdy mesh, sheeting or other material extending at least 900mm up from the surface or the toe board (s 306E(5)(c)) — rails alone are not enough on a pitch.

Fall protection cover over every skylight and opening you will work near, before you work near it: able to withstand the impact of a person falling onto it, and securely fixed so it cannot be moved or removed accidentally (s 306F).
Crawl boards or roof ladders bearing on purlins or structural members wherever fragile sheeting has to be crossed — laid out and walked on, not carried past and forgotten.

Prevention before arrest, in that order, and write it down. Where there is no edge protection and the fall is 2m or more, or the roof slope is over 26°, s 306D(3) requires control measures that PREVENT a person falling any distance — edge protection, a fall protection cover, a travel restraint system — and only if prevention is not practicable, measures to arrest the fall and minimise injury. Section 79(3) ranks the same way: fall prevention device, then work positioning system, then fall arrest. Whatever you land on goes in the s 299(4) record with the reasons.

Treat every fibre cement sheet, every rusted deck sheet and every translucent roof light as fragile. Walk the purlin line, use crawl boards, or do not walk on it at all. Never step or kneel on a skylight — they carry no load and there is nothing under them. If sheeting is likely to be disturbed, that is an s 291(d) asbestos trigger: stop and ring the supervisor.
Two people on the roof, always. No harness is worn alone — s 306I(13). The rescue plan in the last step of this statement assumes a second person because the law does.

No roof work in rain, dew, or wind above the manufacturer's limit for whatever you are using. Get roof work done early in summer, carry water onto the roof, take shade breaks, and come down before you get heat affected — a technician who has stopped sweating comes down now.

Nothing heavy is carried across an unprotected roof by hand. Hoist it, trolley it along the walkway, or split the load and make two trips. A drum or a valve in one arm takes away the arm you need when a sheet goes.

HOLD POINT — this step carries a HIGH residual risk and it does not start on the technician's sign-on alone. It needs the supervisor's sign-off on the day, naming at least one additional control (edge protection hired in, a cover fitted, a different access, out-of-hours work, a second trade), or the job is rebooked with different access. If nobody will sign it, do not walk the roof.

TRAVEL RESTRAINT, when prevention by edge protection or covers is not available: harness and line set SHORT so you physically cannot reach the edge or the fragile sheet. It is harness-based, so it sits at the bottom of the s 79(3) ranking, and it is governed by s 306G, not s 306I — installed by a competent person (s 306G(1)(a)); anchorage point able to withstand any load that could be exerted on it in normal operation of the system (s 306G(1)(b)); the user trained in its safe and correct use (s 306G(2)); no component used that shows wear or weakness to an extent that may affect safety (s 306G(3)); inspected by a competent person at least every 6 months with a written record given to the business (s 306G(4)); the record kept for the lesser of 4 years or the life of the system (s 306G(5)). Measure the line on the roof and lock it off; do not eyeball it.

FALL ARREST, only where prevention and work positioning are both genuinely impracticable. Anchor engineer-designed for the purpose, or inspected and approved by a competent person before first use (s 306I(1)). Anchorage capacity, other than one supporting a static line: at least 12kN for one person with a limited free fall, 15kN for one person with a free fall, 21kN for two people (s 306I(2)). The anchor must be positioned so the lanyard can be attached BEFORE you move into a position where you could fall (s 306I(3)) — clip on at the hatch, before you step out onto the roof, not after. The energy absorber must limit the force applied to you to not more than 6kN (s 306I(4)). Do the clearance sum before you rig anything: your height, the height and position of the anchor, the lanyard length, static line sag, stretch, and absorber extension (s 306I(7) and (8)). A 2m lanyard with an energy absorber typically needs something like 6.5m of clear space below the anchor — a 4m internal warehouse height does not have it, so restraint is the only workable answer in most of the buildings we service. Components inspected by a competent person at least every 6 months with a written record kept (s 306I(10)(c) and (d)).

steps.responsible: Technician (with supervisor sign-off on the day)

steps.step: Sprinkler valves, tank tops and elevated hydrant boosters
hazards: Fall from a tank ladder, tank top or valve platform with no rail
Charged line opened at a valve that indicates shut but is not
Water discharge under pressure into the face when a drain or test valve is cracked
Tank hatch opened, turning a height job into a confined space entry
Lifting a valve, a hose reel drum or a box of heads at height, one-handed, off balance

controls.control: Do not open a tank hatch or put your head into a tank. That is a confined space under AS/NZS 2865 — stop, get the entry permit and the confined space SWMS, and reschedule with the right crew and gas detection. Note that work in or near a confined space is high risk construction work in its own right under s 291(f), so even working on the tank top beside an openable hatch changes what this job is.
Prove the isolation. Crack the drain and watch it run dry before you open anything — the position indicator on a stop valve is not proof.
Work inside the tank top or valve platform guardrail where there is one, and check it is actually edge protection and not a handrail on one side — s 306E sets what a rail has to be.

Where the tank top or valve platform has NO rail, work down the s 79(3) ranking before you reach for a harness. Can the job be done from a fall prevention device — a hired guardrail, a platform, the EWP basket parked alongside? If not, will a WORK POSITIONING SYSTEM do it — plant or a structure that positions and safely supports you at the valve for the duration of the work? That tier sits ABOVE harness-based restraint and this trade routinely skips it. Record which one you chose and why in the s 299(4) list.
Stand out of the line of the drain and the outlet and expect the line to be charged. Open slowly, from the side, with the gauge in sight, and with safety glasses on.

Booster or valve on a wall, podium or dock face: platform ladder, a second person footing it — which is also how the s 306L(3)(b) securing duty is satisfied where you could fall 2m or more — and the area below coned off before you go up.

Nothing heavy goes up or down by hand. Valves, hose reel drums, boxes of heads and extinguishers go on a rope, in the basket at ground level, or on a trolley. Two people on anything awkward, and neither of them on a ladder while they lift it.

Travel restraint off an anchor meeting s 306G, with the line set short of the edge — not a lanyard long enough to reach it. Never alone: where the system is a fall arrest harness system, s 306I(13) prohibits solo use outright.

steps.step: Control everything that can fall from where you are
hazards: Detector head, base ring, spanner, torch or phone dropped from ceiling height onto a person
Rust scale and ceiling dust into the eyes of someone below
Damage to stock, cars or plant under the work

controls.control: Nobody works, walks or parks under the work. That is the whole point of the exclusion zone. Section 54 makes managing the risk of a falling object a duty in its own right, and s 55(3)(a) says the object is prevented from falling freely so far as is reasonably practicable before anything else.

In a live centre, hospital corridor, loading dock or carpark, tape is a warning and not a barrier. Hard barriers, a closed and signed door, or a person stationed at each entry, for the whole time anything is above head height. If you cannot close the area, you work out of hours.
Tool lanyards on every tool that goes above ground level, and a closed pouch for heads, glass bulbs, screws and base rings. Nothing loose in a shirt pocket.
Kick rails and toe boards on the EWP basket kept clear — nothing loose on the platform floor to be kicked over the edge when you turn around.
Lower gear on a rope. Never drop, throw or hand down past a person, and never work directly above another technician.
Hard hats on anyone who genuinely has to be below the work, and they stay outside the barricade the rest of the time.

steps.step: Come down, restore the system and hand the area back
hazards: Isolation left in and the building unprotected overnight
Fire watch stood down before the system is actually back on line
Barricades, hoses and gear left across an egress path
Hatch or roof door left unlocked and open to the public
Ladder or machine left set up for someone else to climb

controls.control: Lock the sprinkler stop valve OPEN with the strap and padlock. Where the valve is monitored, confirm the valve switch has returned to normal at the panel — the monitor is the thing that catches a valve left shut when memory does not, and if the point will not restore the valve is not open, whatever the handwheel looks like. Where the valve is NOT monitored, two people check it: one opens and counts the turns to the backstop, the other reads the pressure gauge and signs the sheet.

Restore the zone or loop at the FIP, ring the brigade connection back on, lift the impairment notice and record the time — before you pack the ute, not from the next job. Print or photograph the panel event log as the record.
Confirm pressure has returned on the gauge, check no head was left disturbed, and only then ring the fire watch and stand them down. The watch stays on until the panel and the valve both read normal.
Clear the barricades and cones, dry any water on the floor, and confirm the egress path is back to normal before the area re-opens.
Lock the hatch and roof door, return the key to the person you got it from, and lower the machine fully with the key out and the isolator off.
Sign off the site, tell the building contact what was isolated and what is still defective, and photograph anything left as a defect for the report.

steps.step: Rescue — agreed before the harness goes on, not after the fall
hazards: Suspension intolerance in a hanging technician within minutes
Technician unconscious or crushed in a basket with nobody trained on the ground controls
Crew standing under the work ringing 000 with no plan and no equipment
Rescuer becoming the second casualty

controls.control: The EWP is the rescue tool: bring the basket down on the ground controls or the emergency lowering valve. That is why the second person stays on the ground and why the pre-start tests the lowering from the ground before anyone goes up.
On a roof, the rescue kit — descender and rope rated for the job, and a means of taking the load off a suspended person — goes ONTO the roof with you. A kit in the ute is not a rescue plan.

Before a harness is worn, the crew agrees out loud who lowers, with what, and from where. Section 80(2) requires emergency procedures, including rescue procedures, to be established for the use of a fall arrest system; s 80(3) requires them to be TESTED so they are effective; s 80(4) requires relevant workers — the person wearing it and anyone who may have to run the rescue — to be given suitable and adequate information, training and instruction in them. If it has not been tested, it is not a rescue plan, and 'we'd call the brigade' does not satisfy s 80.
No harness is worn alone — s 306I(13). Everything below assumes a second person on the ground or on the roof, because the law does.

Get a suspended person down and LYING FLAT as soon as it is safe to do so, and take their weight off the leg straps. Plan on 10 minutes, not as a budget you are allowed to spend: ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.5 reports harness suspension trauma after more than about 10 minutes of suspension, and there is no safe window to wait out. Do not wait at the bottom for QFES.

Lay them flat. The old advice to keep a rescued person sitting upright and off the ground for about 30 minutes has been WITHDRAWN — ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.5 found no evidence supporting it and says it may be harmful. Experienced crew still believe it and will argue; the person running the rescue makes the call and this line is the authority for it.
Ring 000 and the site's emergency contact at the same time as the rescue starts, not instead of it. One person makes the call, another runs the rescue, a third meets the ambulance at the gate.

HOLD POINT — if the tested plan, the rescue kit and the trained second person are not ALL on site, the harness does not go on and the work is rebooked. That is what brings this step down from extreme; without them it is back to extreme and the job stops.

steps.responsible: Supervisor (plan, testing and training under s 80) / Second person on the ground (execution)

emergency:
FALL ARRESTED, PERSON HANGING: do not wait for QFES. Start the rescue now. Plan on getting them down inside 10 minutes — ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.5 reports harness suspension trauma after more than about 10 minutes of suspension and there is no safe window to wait out. Bring the basket down on the ground controls or the emergency lowering valve, or lower them to a surface with the roof rescue kit. Take their weight off the leg straps. LAY THEM FLAT as soon as it is safe — the old instruction to keep a rescued person sitting upright for about 30 minutes has been withdrawn as unsupported and possibly harmful (ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.5); if someone on the crew argues for it, this statement overrules them. Keep them still, keep them warm, and tell 000 "harness suspension trauma after an arrested fall".

PERSON STRUCK BY A DROPPED OBJECT: stop all work above immediately. Do not move them if they are unresponsive or complaining of neck or back pain. Call 000, send someone to the gate.

PERSON CRUSHED BETWEEN THE BASKET AND STRUCTURE: release the basket from the ground controls or the emergency lowering valve, then call 000. Never send a second person up in the same basket.

EWP STUCK ELEVATED WITH A LIVE FAULT: do not climb out. Use the emergency lowering. If it fails, stay in the basket with the harness clipped and call the hire company and 000. Getting out of an elevated basket is what this statement forbids in normal work and it does not become safe in an emergency.

FIRE WHILE THE SYSTEM IS IMPAIRED: the fire watch raises the alarm and calls 000 directly — the brigade connection is off line and the panel will not call for them. Get the isolation restored if it is safe to do so and say on the phone which zones and which sprinkler valves are out.

AFTER ANY OF IT: quarantine and tag out the harness, lanyard and anchor under s 306I(11) — a fall arrest harness system that has been used to arrest a fall must not be used again unless its manufacturer or a competent person has inspected it and decided it is fit for safe use. Quarantine and tag out the ladder, scaffold or machine under the plant duties instead — s 213 requires maintenance, inspection and, if necessary, testing by a competent person, and the s 19 primary duty stands over it; s 306I(11) does not cover plant and should not be cited for it. Leave the site undisturbed so far as is safe: WHS Act s 39 requires the site of a notifiable incident to be preserved until an inspector arrives or the regulator directs otherwise.

NOTIFICATION: the office notifies Workplace Health and Safety Queensland immediately on 1300 362 128. A fall requiring immediate treatment as an in-patient in a hospital is a serious injury under WHS Act s 36 and therefore a notifiable incident under s 35, and so is a dangerous incident under s 37 — which expressly includes the fall or release from a height of any plant, substance or thing, and the collapse, overturning, failure or malfunction of plant required to be authorised for use. A person falling through a roof, a dropped tool that could have killed someone, or an EWP tipping all count even if nobody is hurt.

SITE DETAILS go in the job's JSEA before work starts: assembly point, nearest hospital, who holds the first aid kit and defib, where the rescue kit is, and the building contact's mobile.

What is under 2m on this job and still able to hurt you — a 1.8m platform ladder over a concrete plant room floor, a bench edge, an open riser door — and what is controlling it?
Is anyone working alone today, and does any part of this job require a harness or a roof trip? If yes, who is the second person, and if there isn't one, when is it rebooked for?
Where is the roof access, who holds the key, and what hours can you have it?
Where is the nearest anchor point on this roof, what date is on its inspection record, and who inspected it?
Is any of this roof fibre cement, rusted deck or polycarbonate roof light, and what does the site's asbestos register say about it? If there is no register, what are you doing instead of going up?
What is the internal height under the work, and is there enough clear distance below for a lanyard and energy absorber to deploy — or does it have to be restraint?

Before you reach for a harness on that tank top or valve platform: is there a fall prevention device, or a work positioning system, that would do the job? Write the answer down for the s 299(4) record.
Which FIP, and which zone or loop, are you isolating? Which sprinkler stop valve? Who did you tell, and when does it go back on?
Who is doing the fire watch while the system is down, over what area, at what patrol interval, and what is the agreed maximum impairment time written on the notice?
Who is the second person on the ground today, and are they trained on this machine's ground controls and emergency lowering?
Is the machine rated for outdoor use, what is its wind rating, and where exactly is it going — inside, on a dock, or on an open deck?
Is the slab you are driving the EWP onto suspended, and who confirmed in writing that it will take the machine?
Are there overhead electric lines within reach of the boom, what is their voltage, and what is the schedule 2 exclusion zone for operating plant at that voltage?
What forklift, truck or vehicle movement runs through this aisle or carpark, and who has agreed in writing to stop it while you are up?
Does any part of today's work touch a 240V supply, a mains-connected sounder or a lighting circuit — and if so, which licensed electrical worker is booked?
Are you going above a ceiling today? What is up there, how hot is it, and what is the void wired with?
If you go over the edge or drop in the harness, who gets you down, with what equipment, and from where — and when was that plan last tested?
Which crew members were consulted on this statement, and when? Anything they raised that is not yet in it?
Where does the ambulance come in, who meets it, and where is the assembly point?
