ANNEXURE A to this SWMS — Restore checklist (step 11), item by item, in the same order as the tablet
siteSpecificPrompts: Which FIP, where is it, who holds the key, and is there more than one panel or a sub-panel network on this site? Photograph the panel label and match it to the job before you isolate.
Where is the ASE, and can the brigade signal be isolated at the panel — or does this site need an isolation request to the monitoring contractor first?

What else signals through this ASE besides detection — sprinkler flow and valve monitoring, hydrant or sprinkler pump alarm and fault, gaseous release and fault, lift and plant fault? List it, put it in the written authority, and give it to the fire watch.
Monitoring centre phone number and this site's account / ASE reference — write it on the tablet before you isolate.

Is there any gaseous, special hazard, pre-action or deluge system on this site? Which rooms does it protect, where is the cylinder bank or release valve, who is the contractor, and how is the release physically locked off and verified?
Where are the manual release points for those protected spaces, and how are they covered or isolated?
Who is the chief warden today and what is their mobile? Who is on reception when the phones start ringing?
Who is the named fire watch while the system is isolated, what area do they cover, what is now unmonitored, and how do they raise the alarm? Have you seen them in person?
Agreed isolation-off time, MAXIMUM isolation period, and who rings whom if it is going to slip?
On this panel type, does the detection isolate inhibit manual call points as well? Prove it on the display before you press one.

Is there a current asbestos register for this building, and does it show ACM in any ceiling void, riser, plant room or roof space you need to enter? If there is no register and the building predates 2004, what is your plan?

Which devices are out of reach from the floor, and what access do they actually need: test pole, permanent walkway, mobile scaffold or EWP? For each device where none of those work, what is the recorded reason?
If fall arrest may be used anywhere today: where is the written rescue plan, who is the trained rescuer on site, and what is the means of rescue?
Is any device inside a lift pit, duct, plenum, tank or smoke reservoir? If yes, stop — confined space, different SWMS.
Are any detectors inside ducts or fan housings, and who is isolating and locking out the fan before you put a hand in?
Any detectors in a cold store, freezer room or chiller — artificial extremes of temperature?

Is there powered mobile plant moving through any test area today — forklifts, order pickers, delivery vehicles, cleaning machines? Can the aisle actually be shut, or are you falling back to cones and a spotter?
Where is the FIP's 240 V fire supply isolator, is it labelled, and can it be locked off? What is the battery capacity, and what is your maximum time on battery?

What is on the ancillary cause-and-effect matrix for this site — lifts, AHU, smoke exhaust, stair pressurisation, fire and smoke shutters, door holders, mag locks, gas valves, pre-action or deluge release?
Are the lift contractor, mechanical contractor and special hazard contractor attending for the interface tests, and who are they?
Which areas cannot take sounders at full volume during business hours — theatre, ICU, aged care, child care, call centre, data hall — and what has the FM agreed instead?
What is the measured sound level at the positions you will stand, and which class and type of hearing protector does that give you under AS/NZS 1269.3? Can you still hear the stop word?
Anyone in the affected zones with a known photosensitive epilepsy risk, and has the FM told them before the strobes run?
Who are the persons with special needs in the affected zones, and has the FM and chief warden decided whether they are moved, briefed, or the zone is tested out of hours?

Is any of this test after hours? If so: two technicians confirmed in writing, maximum hours, hours since last shift, lighting, access, lifts, security, and is the fire watch and a contactable FM actually on site tonight?
Is anyone working alone at any point today? What is the check-in interval and who escalates if a check-in is missed?
Does every plant room and riser door you need open from the inside? Do you have the key on your body?
Any other trade on hot work, a sprinkler impairment, or roof work today? Check the permit board.
Where is the first aid kit, the defib, the muster point, and the nearest hospital?
What is the roof access route, is there a walkway, and is any of the roof fragile sheeting?
Open defects from the last service — anything that means part of the system already cannot detect or warn?
Current QFD unwanted alarm charge for this financial year, for the FM's information — look it up on the day, do not quote a figure from an old report.

review.reason: A reviewer read the corrected statement and would not sign it.
findings: [fatal] The hazard 'Contact with a live luminaire, busway or a sprinkler head while reaching' is named and then abandoned. Nothing in the fourteen controls addresses electrical clearance at ceiling level or protection of sprinkler heads.

[fatal] The SWMS makes an EWP the preferred fall prevention device for work at ceiling height in an occupied building, and never once names crush or entrapment between the basket and the overhead structure.

[serious] The SWMS offers 'a mobile scaffold with guardrails' as a primary fall prevention device under s 79(3)(a) and then gives the crew nothing to work to. There is no control for castors locked before anyone climbs, outriggers or stabilisers…

[serious] Wrong part. I pulled the Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld), SL 2008 No. 160, current version. Part 3 is headed 'Occupancy limits for buildings' and contains s 14 'Meaning of occupancy safety factors' and the occupancy-limit…

title: Live sprinkler and wet system — valve work, draining and isolating
activity: Shutting down, draining and working on a live wet sprinkler or combined system: pumps out of auto, monitoring isolated, main and subsidiary stop valves and every other supply locked, alarm valve, retard chamber, pressure switch and drain-down, then proving it back into service.

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(k)
hrcw.text: is carried out on or near energised electrical installations or services

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(a)
hrcw.text: involves a risk of a person falling more than 2m

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(d)
hrcw.text: involves, or is likely to involve, the disturbance of asbestos

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(f)
hrcw.text: is carried out in or near a confined space

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(o)
hrcw.text: is carried out in an area at a workplace in which there is any movement of powered mobile plant

whenRequired:
Any time the water is going off a wet or combined sprinkler system: alarm valve service or overhaul, changing a pressure switch, retard chamber or seat rubber, shutting a subsidiary stop valve for a tenancy, draining a riser, or chasing a leak on the wet side. Fill it in for the ten-minute isolation too — that is the one that gets left shut. Not for dry pipe, pre-action or deluge systems, and not for a pumpset overhaul or booster work; they trip and drain differently and have their own statements. But the pumps are NOT a separate job here: dropping pressure on a wet system is exactly what the fire and jockey pump controllers start on, so this statement puts them out of auto and puts them back. If the isolating valve sits in a below-ground chamber or you have to enter a tank, stop and add the confined space statement.

IS IT CONSTRUCTION WORK? Start from yes. Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 289(2)(e) makes 'the installation, testing or maintenance of an essential service in relation to a structure' construction work, and a sprinkler system is an essential service. Work only falls out of Chapter 6 if it is genuinely 'testing, maintenance or repair work of a minor nature carried out in connection with a structure' (s 289(3)(d)). A short subsidiary valve isolation may well be maintenance of a minor nature and outside the construction work definition — Safe QLD still requires this statement for it, as the method the work is done to, whether or not it is a statutory safe work method statement on that job.

WHICH HIGH RISK CATEGORIES APPLY. s 291(k) (on or near energised electrical installations or services) applies to essentially every job under this statement, because the pressure switch, tamper switch, FIP and pump controllers are all in the valve room. The other four are conditional and you tick them on site: s 291(a) where the valve set, riser or vent point is reached more than 2 m up; s 291(d) where flange gaskets, valve packing or pipe lagging in an older valve room may be asbestos — see the asbestos register step before you strip anything; s 291(f) where the isolating valve is in a pit, chamber or tank; s 291(o) where an EWP, scissor lift or any other powered mobile plant is moving in the area. Cross out on site the ones that do not apply to this job, and add the matching statement for the ones that do. Do not stretch this one over them.
permits: Written impairment approval from the occupier or building manager: what is isolated, what loses protection, start and finish times, who approved it
Alarm monitoring isolation reference from the fire monitoring centre for the FIP zone or ASE isolation

Confirmation in writing of where the drain water may lawfully go — the site's trade waste approval where it goes to sewer, or the building manager's written direction. Stormwater is not automatically acceptable

Confined space entry permit, and the Safe QLD confined space statement, where the isolating valve is in a pit or chamber or a tank has to be entered (Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), Part 4.3)
Hot work permit and the Safe QLD hot work statement if any cutting, grinding, brazing or welding on the pipework forms part of the job

Energised electrical work authorisation and the Safe QLD electrical statement if anything inside the pressure switch, tamper switch or a controller enclosure has to be opened — that work is not done under this statement
ppe: Safety boots, waterproof, steel cap
Long sleeves and hi-vis
Safety glasses; goggles once a drain is running
Cut-resistant gloves for valve internals and old seat rubbers
P2 disposable respirators, at least two per person — for the drain-down and venting of a stagnant riser. Fit-checked each time you put one on, and it does not seal over a beard
Hearing protection for the water motor gong and in the pump room
Waterproof over-trousers or wet weather gear for the drain-down
Hard hat where work is overhead or under an open riser

Boom-type EWP: full body harness to AS/NZS 1891.1:2020 with a short restraint lanyard, adjusted so you cannot get your feet off the floor of the basket, clipped to the manufacturer's designated anchor point only, selected and used to AS/NZS 1891.4:2025. NOT a twin-tail fall-arrest lanyard — a 2 m twin-tail lets you be thrown over the rail and then arrested outside the basket, and in a plant room you will not have the clearance under you for it to work anyway
Scissor lift: the guardrails are the fall protection. No harness unless the machine's own manufacturer requires one — check the plate before you clip to anything
training: QBCC fire protection occupational licence — water-based fire system, in the class covering the work being done (inspect and test, or install and maintain — commercial)
Plumbing and Drainage Act 2018 (Qld) licence where the work is regulated plumbing work on the water-based system

Licensed electrical worker for any work inside the pressure switch, tamper switch or controller enclosure — Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld). Putting a controller selector to OFF or MANUAL from the outside of the door is not electrical work; opening the door is
Construction induction card (white card), CPCCWHS1001
Provide first aid, HLTAID011, and CPR currency for anyone working near the pump controller
EWP: yellow card for a scissor lift or boom under 11m; WP high risk work licence for a boom-type EWP 11m and over
Working at heights and harness competency, including restraint technique in a boom basket, where the valve set or riser vent is above 2m
Asbestos awareness for anyone stripping gaskets, packing or lagging at a valve set — enough to recognise suspect material and stop

Audiometric testing: anyone who relies on hearing protection against noise above the exposure standard in a pump or valve room is on the audiometric testing program — within 3 months of starting the work and at least every 2 years (Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 58)
Confined space entry and standby training where the isolating valve is in a pit — that work goes to the confined space statement, not this one
Company sign-off on the alarm valve model being serviced, against the manufacturer's instructions

steps.step: Get the impairment approved before a valve is touched
hazards: Building or a tenancy left without sprinkler cover and nobody told
Occupier in breach of the duty to maintain the installation at all times
Unwanted brigade turnout and a false alarm charge from your own test signal
Impairment running past the agreed window into an unattended building

controls.control: Sequence the job so the system spends the least possible time off: everything that can be done live is done live first — external inspection, gauge readings, block plan check, parts laid out and counted. The valve gets shut once, for the shortest time that does the job.

Written approval to impair from the occupier or building manager on the Safe QLD impairment form: system, area losing protection, start and finish time, approver's name and the mobile they are actually on today.

Ring the fire monitoring centre BEFORE anything is isolated and get an isolation reference and the operator's name. Make that call from where you have signal — outside, or in the lobby — because you will not have signal at the valve set. Never isolate the ASE just to stop an unwanted alarm: the occupier's duty is to maintain every prescribed fire safety installation at all times to a standard of safety and reliability in the event of fire (Fire Services Act 1990 (Qld) s 146M), and the answer to repeat unwanted alarms is to fix the cause, not to switch the monitoring off (s 146N).

Agree the interim measures with the occupier and write them on the form: hot work and any grinding on site stopped for the window, fire watch nominated by name, extra extinguishers out, tenants of the affected floors told.
Seat rubbers, gaskets, clapper kit and a spare pressure switch in the van before the valve is shut. No parts run mid-impairment.

steps.step: Identify the system and prove which valve you are about to shut
hazards: Shutting the wrong valve and dropping protection off a tenancy that is not on the permit
Valve set feeding more than one riser or a neighbouring building
Treating a pre-action, deluge or antifreeze loop as a plain wet system
Isolating at a point that also kills the hydrant supply
A supply you have not found yet — a booster, a bypass, a tank and pump — that can put the water back on you later

controls.control: Read the block plan and the valve chart at the valve set, then walk the riser and match it to the ground. Read the alarm valve nameplate — make and model — and check the log book baseline data before you touch a handwheel.

Walk the whole supply, not just the valve you came for. Write down every point that can put water into the section you intend to open: town main, tank and pump, alarm valve bypass, any cross-connection to hydrants, and the fire brigade booster inlet. That written list is what gets locked in the isolation step, and it is what you check back against at handback.

Prove the valve rather than assume it: crack the alarm test valve and watch which gauge and which zone responds. If the gauge and the zone do not agree with the block plan, the plan is wrong and the job stops until you know which valve is which.
Photograph the valve set, both gauges, every valve position and both pump controller selectors as you found them. Those photos are how it goes back.
Where the valve set also feeds hydrants or a second building, confirm the scope with the building manager in person before shutting anything.

steps.step: Set the valve room up and sort out where the water is going
hazards: Wet floor, slips and a hose across the only exit
Discharge finding a switchroom, lift pit, basement carpark or the tenancy below
Water motor gong and FIP sounders at close range
Poor lighting and tight access around the riser
Working alone in a locked plant room with no signal
Hundreds to thousands of litres of contaminated riser water, and any glycol from an antifreeze loop, going somewhere it is not lawful to put it

controls.control: Run the drain to the designated drain point on a hose clamped at both ends. Nothing discharges to the plant room floor and finds its own way out.

Bund or plug the doorway with a sandbag or an absorbent snake, and have the wet vac in the room and plugged in — not in the van — before any water runs. If the only thing between the water and the switchroom is a squeegee, you are not set up.
Task light on the valve set. The plant room fluoro over the door is not enough to read a gauge by, and you will be reading gauges to decide whether it is safe to open a cover.

Check where the drain actually discharges, and that it will take a full main drain without backing up. Run it for a minute and watch it before you commit. If it will not take it, the job does not start until there is a drain that will, or the water is being tankered.

Confirm the drain point is a LAWFUL discharge for this water — stormwater is not automatically acceptable. Black riser water carrying corrosion inhibitor, and any glycol off an antifreeze loop, is contained and disposed of as trade waste, not flushed to stormwater. You must take all reasonably practicable measures to prevent or minimise environmental harm (Environmental Protection Act 1994 (Qld) s 319, general environmental duty), and discharge to sewer needs the local water authority's trade waste approval. If nobody on site can tell you which it is, ring the office before you open the drain.
Barricade the valve set, wet floor signs out, and keep the path to the door clear the whole time. The hose does not cross the exit.

Tell the office where you are and set a call-in time. Working alone in a plant room with no phone signal gets a second person instead — this is not negotiable on a job where you will be draining a riser.
Hearing protection on before the gong runs, waterproofs on before the drain opens.

steps.step: Isolate the monitoring and put the pumps out of auto — before any pressure comes off
hazards: Fire pump or jockey pump starting on falling pressure and running deadheaded against a shut or drained system — overheating, cooked seals and packing, and a diesel set that keeps running until somebody physically stops it
Brigade attending on a tamper, flow or low-pressure signal you generated
Live 240 V and above at the pressure switch enclosure, tamper switch, jockey pump and fire pump controller
Fire pump controller holding supply from more than one source, with the starter still live after the isolator is off
Monitoring or a pump left isolated after you drive off

controls.control: On a pumped system, put the fire pump and the jockey pump controllers OUT OF AUTO at the controller selector, and hang your tag on each, BEFORE any pressure is allowed to fall. The selector is on the outside of the door — you do not open a controller door to do this. Photograph each selector after you move it. If a controller cannot be taken out of auto without opening it, stop: that is the electrician's job, or it goes to the pumpset statement.
Put the FIP zone into isolate before anything else moves, so the monitored tamper, flow switch or low-pressure signal does not send the brigade. Write the zone number on this SWMS.

If anything at all has to be opened — the pressure switch enclosure, the tamper switch, a controller door — it is isolated at the board, locked and tagged by the licensed electrical worker, and proved de-energised by that person, not by you. Every exposed part is treated as energised until it has been isolated and found not to be energised, and de-energised equipment is kept from being inadvertently re-energised while the work is on (Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld), Part 8, Division 3 — electrical work on or near energised electrical equipment).

Do not open the fire pump controller. It can be fed from more than one supply and the starter can stay live with the isolator off. That is the electrician's door, and this statement does not cover opening it.

Disconnecting or reconnecting pressure switch or tamper switch wiring is electrical work under the Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld) and a licensed electrical worker does it. Note also that once a cover is off, 'near' means within 3 metres of an exposed energised part — everyone standing inside that distance is in energised electrical work, not just the person with their hands in it (Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld), Part 8, Division 3). Use the Safe QLD electrical statement for that work; do not run it under this one.
Ring the monitoring centre from where you have signal, get the isolation reference and the operator's name, and write both on this SWMS. It goes back on the same day, by the same reference.
Label the FIP and each pump controller so anyone walking in can read what is isolated or out of auto, who did it, their mobile, and when it is coming back.

steps.responsible: Technician, and a licensed electrical worker for anything inside an enclosure

steps.step: Shut and lock every water supply into the section you are going to open
hazards: Someone reopening a valve while your hand is inside the alarm valve
Re-pressurisation from a supply you never isolated — the fire brigade booster inlet, an alarm valve bypass, the tank and pump, or a hydrant cross-connection
The brigade charging the booster during the impairment and pressurising an open alarm valve
Valve passing or not fully shutting, so the system is still live when you think it is dead
Tamper switch tripping the brigade as the valve closes
Hydraulic shock from slamming a butterfly valve shut
Isolating valve in a below-ground pit

controls.control: Take the list you wrote at identification and shut every supply on it — town main, tank and pump, alarm valve bypass, hydrant cross-connection and the fire brigade booster inlet. Close each one slowly by hand. No bar, no rattle gun. Count the turns on the stop valve and write the number on this SWMS; that number is how you prove it fully open again.

Your own padlock and your own danger tag — name, mobile, date — on EVERY point you shut, not just the main stop valve. One key each, in your pocket, and nobody takes a lock off but the person whose name is on it. If you do not have a lock for every point on the list, you do not have an isolation: get more locks before the job starts.

Where a point will not take a padlock, use a lockable valve strap, a chain and lock, or take the handwheel off and put it in the van — and tag it either way. A tag on its own is a message, not an isolation.

Tag the fire brigade booster inlet 'IMPAIRED — SYSTEM OPEN, DO NOT CHARGE', and tell both the monitoring centre and the building manager that the booster is not to be charged until the impairment is closed out. If the brigade attends for any reason during the impairment, the technician meets them at the booster and tells them the system is open BEFORE any connection is made.

Before the handwheel moves, say it out loud and tick it off: FIP zone isolated, monitoring reference written down, fire and jockey pumps out of auto and tagged, every supply on the list accounted for.

Prove the isolation at the test and drain valve — open it and watch it die. If water keeps coming, something is passing or it is the wrong valve. Stop and find it. Do not open an alarm valve on a maybe.

If any isolating valve is in a below-ground chamber, pit or tank, stop here. That is a confined space: separate permit, the Safe QLD confined space statement and Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) Part 4.3. Do not lean in, do not reach in.

steps.step: Drain down and prove the pressure is gone
hazards: Stored pressure in the riser — a cover or flange letting go under 1000 kPa
Hundreds of litres of black stagnant riser water, aerosolised by the drain and the vent — Legionella is the named risk in stagnant fire water systems, along with other bacteria and endotoxin
Water damage to the tenancy or switchboard below
Drain hose whipping off or the drain not keeping up
A head of water still sitting above a closed clapper while the lower gauge reads zero

controls.control: Hose clamped at both ends, run flat to the drain point and physically restrained at the discharge. A drain hose is never left loose to whip.
Crack the auxiliary drain and open a vent high on the riser so it drains instead of holding a vacuum.
Open the main drain valve slowly and throttle it so the drain point keeps up. If the drain starts to back up, close down until it clears — do not walk away from an open main drain.
Both gauges at zero AND no flow at an open drain before a single bolt is loosened. A zero on the supply gauge alone tells you nothing about what the clapper is holding above you.
Back the alarm valve cover bolts off two turns, stand to the side — not in front of the cover — and watch. Any weep and it is not drained: close it up and drain again.
Riser water is not clean water. Cover cuts before you start, keep it out of your mouth and eyes, and wash your hands before you eat, drink, smoke or touch your phone.

P2 respirator on before the drain is opened, and kept on while the drain is running hard or the riser is being vented — and any time the water is visibly black or smells. Fit-check it each time; it will not seal over a beard. Change it if it gets wet.
Goggles rather than glasses once a drain is running, waterproofs, gloves.

steps.step: Open the valve and do the work
hazards: Alarm valve cover and clapper assembly weight, dropped or pinched fingers
Sharp seat edges, perished rubber, rust and sludge
Asbestos in flange gaskets, valve packing or pipe lagging at the valve set in an older building
Dropped tools onto the person below or into the valve body
Awkward reach and poor footing in a tight valve room
Valve set, riser or vent point reached more than 2 m up

controls.control: Support the cover on a stand or lower it to the floor before you start fitting parts. Do not hold a cover with one hand and work with the other.

Where the work is above 2 m, work off a rated industrial platform ladder or an EWP with the Safe QLD heights statement attached — a fall prevention device first, and a work positioning or fall arrest system only where a fall prevention device is not reasonably practicable (Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) ss 78 and 79, and the hierarchy in s 79(3)). A rung ladder with two hands full is not a work platform.

STOP AND CHECK THE ASBESTOS REGISTER before you strip any gasket, packing, mastic or lagging at the valve set. The person with management or control of the workplace has to have one and keep it current (Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 425) — ask the building manager for it and read it. If the register is silent, or the material is unidentified in a building of an age to have asbestos in it, presume it is asbestos: do not scrape it, do not wire-brush it, do not cut it. Stop, report it, and the work goes to the Safe QLD asbestos statement and a licensed removalist if it has to come off.
Second person takes the weight on any cover or clapper you cannot lift square with both hands. Agree who is lifting and who is guiding before you take the last bolt out.

Manufacturer's service instructions for that exact valve model DOWNLOADED onto the phone before you walk into the plant room — there is no signal at the valve set and clapper orientation and seat torque are model-specific. If you did not download it, go back out and get it.
Tool lanyards, a bucket for parts, nothing loose on the platform. Count what goes into the valve body and count what comes out.
Cut-resistant gloves and eye protection; sleeves down around the seat and springs.

steps.step: Refill, vent and re-pressurise
hazards: Water hammer cracking a fitting or a gauge when the main valve is thrown open
Air slug driving the clapper and running the gong and the brigade signal
Re-pressurising while a cover is still off or someone is still on the riser
A pump coming back to auto too early and slamming a part-filled riser
Leaks at your own joint dripping into the tenancy overnight

controls.control: Fill through the bypass or the priming line with the main stop valve still shut. Never refill a drained riser by cracking the main valve.
Vent at the high point until you get clean water with no air, then close the vent. Air left in the riser is what trips the alarm on refill and what cracks fittings.
Covers on, bolts pulled up diagonally to the manufacturer's torque, everyone's hands clear and CALLED clear — out loud, answered — before water goes back in.

The fire and jockey pumps stay OUT OF AUTO through the whole refill. They go back in the next step, after the stop valve is proved fully open. A jockey cutting in on a part-filled riser is how you finish the day with a cracked gauge.
Open the main stop valve a quarter turn at a time and watch the downstream gauge climb. Stop and look at every leak you hear.
Refill the retard chamber priming water and check the alarm line drain is clear so the gong does not run on you.
Walk the affected area and look up: weeping heads, dripping joints, ceiling tiles staining. Find it now, not from the tenant's phone call at 6am.

steps.step: Prove the system, put the pumps back in auto and the monitoring back on
hazards: Stop valve left part shut, so the system looks in service and is not
System handed back with the fire pump or jockey pump left out of auto — the alarm test at the valve set passes and nobody notices
A lock or tag left on the booster, a bypass or the tank supply
Pressure switch, tamper or flow switch not proving after the work
System handed back with the FIP zone still isolated
Pressures down on baseline and written off as normal

controls.control: Open the stop valve FULLY — OS&Y stem all the way back, or the same number of turns you counted closing it — then strap and lock it open and put the tamper switch back in service.

Fire pump and jockey pump controllers back to AUTO. Confirm each selector by eye, photograph it against the arrival photo, and then stand there and watch the jockey cut in and cut out on its own pressure settings. Record the jockey start and stop pressures and the fire pump start pressure against the log book baseline. The alarm test valve proves the alarm chain — it does not prove the pump, so the pump gets proved separately, here, every time.

Walk the isolation list you wrote and point at every single point on it: booster, bypass, tank and pump, hydrant cross-connection, main stop valve. Every lock off, every tag off, every valve back where the arrival photo shows it. The booster 'DO NOT CHARGE' tag comes off too, and the monitoring centre and the building manager are told the booster is available again.
Run the alarm test valve and prove the whole chain: water motor gong, pressure switch, FIP alarm, signal received at the monitoring centre. No signal at the centre, no sign-off.
Record static and running pressures and compare them with the baseline in the log book. A drop against baseline is a defect to investigate, not a number to write down and leave.
De-isolate the FIP zone, ring the monitoring centre, confirm the system reads normal at their end, and write down the de-isolation reference, the operator's name and the time.
Take your own padlock and tag off yourself, last, once the tests have passed.

steps.step: Close out and hand the system back
hazards: Lock or tag left on a valve
Impairment left open in the site records
A defect found during the work left unreported
Occupier never told the system is back in service
Water and barricades left for the cleaner

controls.control: Impairment start and finish times, every isolation point and its release, valve turns, pump selector positions, parts fitted and test results into the AS 1851 log book and onto the job before you leave the plant room.

Critical defect is a TWO-LIMB test and both limbs have to be met (Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 49): the defect is likely to render the installation inoperable, AND it is reasonably likely to have a significant adverse impact on the safety of occupants of part or all of the building if a fire or hazardous materials emergency happens. A sprinkler system or a floor left out of service will normally meet both. One dud extinguisher among several will not. Where both limbs are met, s 53 requires a critical defect notice in the approved form to the occupier WITHIN 24 HOURS AFTER YOU CARRY OUT THE MAINTENANCE — the clock runs from the maintenance, not from when you got round to noticing — and the interim measures go in writing with it.
Tell the occupier's contact in person or by phone that the system is back on, and confirm it in writing the same day. A text message with the time on it counts; assuming they know does not.

Squeegee and mop, pull the barricades, and photograph the valve set, the gauges and both pump controller selectors as you left them against the photos you took on arrival. Compare them before you get in the van.

steps.step: If the system cannot go back in service today
hazards: Building or tenancy unprotected overnight with nobody watching
Occupier believing the system is in service when it is not
Monitoring left isolated with no reference and no end date
A fire pump left in auto against a shut valve, running deadheaded overnight and destroying itself
Hot work or a fit-out continuing under dead heads

controls.control: Do not start a job you cannot finish inside the window. Parts not on hand, second person gone, or the window nearly up — the valve stays open, the pumps stay in auto, and the work is rebooked. This is the control that actually works; everything below it is damage limitation.

If the water is staying off overnight, the fire and jockey pumps stay OUT OF AUTO and stay tagged. A pump in auto against a shut valve will run deadheaded and destroy itself, and on a diesel set it will keep running. Write on the FIP label and on the defect notice that the pumps are out of auto as well as the water being off, so whoever comes back knows there are two things to restore.
Ring the supervisor BEFORE the window closes, not after. The decision to leave a building impaired overnight is not a technician's alone.

Written notice to the occupier: what is out of service, which area loses cover, that the pumps are out of auto, and the interim measures — fire watch by the occupier with a name and a phone number, all hot work stopped, extra extinguishers, evacuation plan reviewed with the tenants.

Critical defect notice in the approved form within 24 hours after the maintenance (Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) ss 49 and 53) — a system left out of service overnight will normally satisfy both limbs of the s 49 test. Monitoring stays isolated only with the centre's reference, an end date, and the FIP clearly labelled at the panel.
Return visit booked before you leave site, and the job left on the board as IMPAIRED until it is proved back on — water, monitoring and pumps, all three.

emergency:
FIRE WHILE THE SYSTEM IS ISOLATED — this is the one the impairment exists to worry about. Ring 000 first. Then, if it is safe to reach the valve, RESTORE THE WATER IMMEDIATELY: your lock off, the stop valve wound fully open, every other supply you isolated reopened, the pumps back to AUTO, the FIP zone de-isolated, and the monitoring centre told the system is back on. Restoring protection beats finishing the work — the job is abandoned where it stands and the valve set is left safe. Tell the fire watch and the building warden whether the system is restored or could not be restored, and tell the brigade the same thing the moment they arrive. If the booster was tagged DO NOT CHARGE, pull that tag as part of restoring the system and say so.

ACCIDENTAL DISCHARGE OR A HEAD LET GO, WITH NO FIRE — and confirm there is no fire before you touch anything. Then shut the stop valve you have just been working on: you know where it is and it is not yet locked open. NEVER shut a stop valve on flowing heads while there is any sign of fire, or any alarm you cannot account for. Sprinklers flowing on a fire are doing their job, and shutting them has killed people. If you are in any doubt at all, leave the water on, ring 000, and let the brigade direct the shutdown. Wedge or stop the head only once the water is off. Keep water out of switchrooms and lift shafts; if a board is wet, nobody touches it and the building's electrician isolates it. Get the wet vac and squeegees going, photograph the damage, and ring the office before you start cleaning up. If the brigade is on the way, meet them at the booster with the block plan and tell them exactly what is isolated.

INJURY. First aid from the kit in the van. Ring 000 for anything worse than a cut. Do not move a person hit by a falling valve cover. Contaminated riser water in an eye or an open cut goes to a doctor the same day — say it was stagnant fire system water and that Legionella is a consideration. Notify the office immediately.

NOTIFIABLE INCIDENTS. A death, a serious injury or illness, or a dangerous incident is notifiable to the regulator immediately (Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) s 38). A dangerous incident includes an uncontrolled escape of a pressurised substance and an electric shock (s 37) — an alarm valve cover letting go under pressure, or a shock off a pressure switch, is notifiable whether or not anyone was hurt. WHSQ on 1300 362 128 straight away. The site where the incident occurred is then preserved so far as is reasonably practicable until an inspector arrives or an inspector directs otherwise (s 39). Section 39(3) expressly does not prevent action to assist an injured person, to remove a deceased person, or that is essential to make the site safe or to minimise the risk of a further notifiable incident — so shutting off water, having a wet board isolated and stopping further flooding are all permitted, and you do them. Photograph the scene before you move anything you have to move, and move nothing you do not have to.

SITE EVACUATION. Leave the tools, go to the assembly area named on this SWMS, and tell the warden immediately that the sprinklers are isolated and which areas have no cover.
references: Codes of practice and standards below: confirm the current edition before this statement is issued — Queensland codes are reissued and retitled, and Australian Standards are superseded. Queensland codes are on worksafe.qld.gov.au.

Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) — primary duty of care; s 37 (meaning of dangerous incident); s 38 (duty to notify of notifiable incidents); s 39 (duty to preserve incident sites, and the s 39(3) exceptions for assisting an injured person and making the site safe)

Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 289(2)(e) — the installation, testing or maintenance of an essential service in relation to a structure is construction work; s 289(3)(d) — testing, maintenance or repair work of a minor nature carried out in connection with a structure is not
Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 291 — meaning of high risk construction work; the categories relied on here are s 291(a), (d), (f), (k) and (o)

Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) ss 299, 300, 302 and 303 — safe work method statement required, compliance with it, review, and the duty to keep it (until the work is complete, and at least 2 years after a notifiable incident). Note s 299(4): where the only fall controls are administrative or PPE, the statement must describe all control measures considered, addressing s 79(3)
Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) ss 78 and 79 — management of the risk of a fall, and the s 79(3) hierarchy: fall prevention device, then work positioning system, then fall arrest system

Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) Part 4.3, ss 62 to 77 — confined spaces: entry permit, risk assessment and record keeping, where an isolating valve is in a pit or chamber or a tank must be entered

Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 58 — audiometric testing for workers required to use hearing protection against noise above the exposure standard: within 3 months of starting the work and at least every 2 years
Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 425 — the asbestos register the person with management or control of the workplace must prepare, keep and maintain at the workplace
How to manage work health and safety risks Code of Practice 2021 (Qld)
Managing the risk of falls at workplaces Code of Practice 2021 (Qld)
Confined spaces Code of Practice 2021 (Qld)
Managing risks of plant in the workplace Code of Practice 2021 (Qld)
Managing noise and preventing hearing loss at work Code of Practice 2021 (Qld)
First aid in the workplace Code of Practice 2021 (Qld)

Workplace Health and Safety Queensland code of practice on managing and controlling asbestos in the workplace — check the current title and year on worksafe.qld.gov.au before issue; suspected asbestos on this work is a stop work and goes to the Safe QLD asbestos statement, not to this one
Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld) — what is electrical work, and who may perform it

Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld), SL 2026 No. 113 (commenced 1 September 2026) — Part 8, Division 3, electrical work on or near energised electrical equipment: 'near' means within 3 m of an exposed energised part; every exposed part is treated as energised until isolated and found not to be energised; de-energised equipment must not be inadvertently re-energised while work is on. This regulation replaced the repealed Electrical Safety Regulation 2013 (Qld); any document still citing the 2013 regulation is out of date

Fire Services Act 1990 (Qld) s 146M — the occupier of a building must maintain at all times every prescribed fire safety installation to a standard of safety and reliability in the event of fire (relocated and renumbered from s 104D by 2024 No. 22 s 56(2))

Fire Services Act 1990 (Qld) s 146N — the occupier must maintain each monitored system so that an unacceptable number of unwanted alarms are not signalled from it. The answer to repeat unwanted alarms is to fix the cause, not to isolate the ASE

Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 49 (meaning of critical defect — both limbs must be met), s 50 (maintenance in compliance with QDC part MP6.1) and s 53 (critical defect notice in the approved form to the occupier within 24 hours after the maintenance is carried out)

Environmental Protection Act 1994 (Qld) s 319 — general environmental duty: a person must not carry out an activity that causes, or is likely to cause, environmental harm unless all reasonably practicable measures are taken to prevent or minimise it. Applies to where riser water, corrosion inhibitor and glycol are discharged. Discharge to sewer additionally needs the local water authority's trade waste approval
Queensland Development Code, Mandatory Part 6.1 — Maintenance of fire safety installations

AS 1851-2012 Routine service of fire protection systems and equipment, incorporating Amendment 1:2016 — the sprinkler systems section for the routine service schedule, and clause 1.16.2 for critical defects. The sprinkler section number is deliberately not quoted here: Safe QLD's standards register only carries section and clause numbers read off the company's own copy, because citing the wrong section on a service record is worse than citing none. Read the section number off the copy in the office before you write it on a record. Note also that what AS 1851 calls a critical defect is NOT the same test as the two-limb test in Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 49 — keep them separate
AS 2118.1:2017 Automatic fire sprinkler systems, Part 1: General systems, incorporating Amendments 1:2017, 2:2020 and 3:2024 — valve set arrangement, stop valves secured open

AS 1670.1:2024 Fire detection, warning, control and intercom systems — System design, installation and commissioning, Part 1: Fire (supersedes AS 1670.1:2018) — for the fire indicator panel and the zone isolate function

AS 1670.3:2024 Fire detection, warning, control and intercom systems — System design, installation and commissioning, Part 3: Fire alarm monitoring — for the alarm signalling equipment and the path to the monitoring centre

AS/NZS 1891.1:2020 Personal equipment for work at height, Part 1: Manufacturing requirements for full body combination and lower body harnesses

AS/NZS 1891.4:2025 Personal equipment for work at height, Part 4: Selection, use and maintenance (supersedes AS/NZS 1891.4:2009) — harness and lanyard selection, including restraint rather than fall arrest in a boom basket, and inspection intervals
AS 2550.10:2025 Cranes, hoists and winches — Safe use, Part 10: Mobile elevating work platforms (supersedes AS 2550.10-2006)
