Manufacturer's service instructions for the alarm valve model fitted, and for the pumpset controllers on site
siteSpecificPrompts: Which valve set are you isolating, and what else does it feed besides the area you are working in?

List every supply that can pressurise the section you will open — town main, tank and pump, alarm valve bypass, hydrant cross-connection, booster inlet. How many locks and tags do you need, and do you have that many on the van?
Is this system pumped? Where are the fire and jockey pump controllers, and can you reach the AUTO selector on each without opening a door?
Where is the fire brigade booster inlet, who is tagging it, and who has told the monitoring centre and the building manager it is not to be charged?
Where does the drain discharge to, and will it take a full main drain without flooding anything?
Is the drain point stormwater or sewer, and does the site hold a trade waste approval for this discharge? Is there glycol or corrosion inhibitor in this water?
Who is the occupier's contact approving the impairment, and what mobile are they on today?
What time does the impairment start and what time have you agreed it ends?
What is the monitoring centre's isolation reference, the operator's name, and which FIP zone is isolated?
Which tenancies or areas lose sprinkler cover while the valve is shut, and who has told them?
Is any hot work, grinding or fit-out running on site during the window, and has it been stopped in writing?
How old is this building, and have you seen the asbestos register for the valve room before you strip a gasket, packing or lagging?
What are the static and running pressures on the gauges before you touch anything, what are the pump start and stop pressures, and what does the log book baseline say they should be?
Is any part of this job more than 2 m up, and if so what are you standing on — and is any powered mobile plant moving in the area?
Where is the assembly area, the nearest hose reel and the site first aid kit, and who is on fire watch while the system is down?

review.reason: The second review never ran — the run that would have read this statement stopped before reaching it. Nobody has checked whether the corrections landed.

title: Working alone, in carparks and near traffic
activity: One technician on their own servicing fire equipment in basement carparks, on street frontages and at boosters, with no second person on site.

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(a)
hrcw.text: involves a risk of a person falling more than 2m

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(f)
hrcw.text: is carried out in or near a confined space

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(n)
hrcw.text: is carried out on, in or adjacent to a road, railway, shipping lane or other traffic corridor that is in use by traffic other than pedestrians

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(o)
hrcw.text: is carried out in an area at a workplace in which there is any movement of powered mobile plant

whenRequired:
Any day one technician is on a site on their own, and any time part of the work sits on a road frontage, a footpath, a driveway crossover, or inside a carpark with vehicles moving through it. Booster services, hydrant flow tests at the street, carpark detectors and heads, basement plant rooms, and after-hours call-outs. Fill it in for a half-hour job as well as a full day: the exposure is the aisle and the frontage, not the length of the visit.

Be honest about where the high-risk line sits, because a technician will be asked. Routine servicing of a fire system is the maintenance of an essential service in relation to a structure, which is construction work under s 289(2)(e) of the Regulation, and s 291 then makes it high risk construction work where it is carried out adjacent to a road in use by traffic, where powered mobile plant is moving, where there is a risk of a person falling more than 2 m, or where it is carried out in or near a confined space. But s 289(3)(d) carves testing, maintenance or repair work of a minor nature out of construction work altogether, so a five-minute extinguisher check in a quiet carpark is not HRCW and does not need this statement signed to be lawful. A booster service on a live road frontage, a shift spent in an aisle with cars moving through it, or a carpark head reached off a ladder, is.

WHAT A LONE TECHNICIAN MAY AND MAY NOT DO UNDER THIS STATEMENT. Three hard lines, and they decide whether today is a lone visit at all.
1. Traffic. A lone technician works behind the kerb line, or on a footpath that is properly closed. Any work zone that puts a person or a device in a trafficked lane is a two-person job. A lone technician never places, adjusts or retrieves a cone, a sign or a barrier in a live lane — see Step 6 for what you may do and Step 7 for the crewed version.
2. Height. Work from the ground, from a platform step ladder within its rated standing height, or from a low platform is covered by Step 9. Work where a fall of more than 2 m is possible is not done alone: there is nobody to foot the ladder, steady the platform, or raise the alarm, and a fall arrest system is no answer when there is nobody to rescue you off it. That work goes to a crewed visit under the working-at-height SWMS, where s 79(3) sets the order of protection — a fall prevention device first, then a work positioning system, then a fall arrest system.
3. Confined spaces. No entry on a lone visit, ever — see Step 10. The Regulation requires continuous communication with the worker from outside the space and a standby person in the vicinity of it before anyone enters (part 4.3, s 69). A lone technician has neither, by definition, so the entry is neither lawful nor survivable.

Where the work is HRCW, s 299 requires this statement to exist before the work starts, and s 299(2)(d) requires it to describe how the controls are implemented, MONITORED and REVIEWED — see the review clause below. s 300(1) requires the company to have arrangements in place so the work is carried out the way this statement says; s 300(2) requires that if it is not being carried out that way, the work is stopped immediately or as soon as it is safe to do so, and resumed only in accordance with this statement. Under s 303 the statement is kept until the work is complete, is readily accessible to the technician doing the work (on the tablet, on site, while the work is going on), is available for inspection under the Act, and is kept for at least 2 years if a notifiable incident happens in connection with the work.

Principal contractor. Where the work is part of a construction project — construction work costing $250,000 or more (s 292) — a copy must be given to the principal contractor before the work starts (s 301). Routine service work is almost never a construction project, so on most visits there is no principal contractor at all. Do not go looking for one; if you are inducted onto a site that has one, give them a copy.

REVIEW OF THIS STATEMENT (s 299(2)(d) and s 302). The WHS supervisor owns this statement and reviews it with the technicians who work to it. It is reviewed and revised whenever control measures are revised under s 38, and specifically: after any incident or near miss on this work; whenever a technician stops work under s 300(2); when a control is found not to be working; when a site, its traffic arrangement, its lighting or its ventilation changes; when the Queensland temporary traffic management framework or its accreditations change; and in any case at least every 12 months. The monitoring input is the site record the technician fills in at check-out (Step 14) — lighting, reception and what communications actually worked, boom gate, traffic peak, plant room noise level, ventilation, and the defects raised. The supervisor reads those, they are not just filed.
permits: Road corridor permit from the local council, or a Department of Transport and Main Roads road corridor permit where the frontage is a state-controlled road — in hand before the first cone goes out

Approved Traffic Guidance Scheme, prepared by an accredited traffic management designer, where any part of the work or the work zone sits in a trafficked lane or on the footpath. If the scheme puts any device in a live lane, this is not a lone visit — it is rebooked as a crewed shift (Step 7)
Building manager's after-hours access authority, with keys or fob signed out and signed back
Carpark bay or loading zone booking where the work occupies a bay or an aisle

Impairment notice to the monitoring company and the building's fire safety adviser where the testing takes any part of the system off line — and the matching clearance call before you leave site (Step 14). The impairment is not closed until you have their reference number written on the job

Confined space entry permit — never available on a lone visit. If the work needs entry to a booster or hydrant pit, a tank hatch, a pump well or any other confined space, stop and rebook it as a crewed visit under the confined space SWMS and permit (Regulation part 4.3)
ppe: Class D/N high-visibility garment to AS/NZS 4602.1:2011 — worn in the carpark as well as on the street
Lace-up safety boots with a toe cap to AS/NZS 2210.3:2019, soles wiped clean of grease before any ladder work
Head torch and a separate hand torch, both charged that morning — a phone torch is not the plan
Safety glasses to AS/NZS 1337.1:2010 for booster caps, valve glands and anything that has been under pressure — worn after the line is drained and proved at zero, never instead of draining it
General purpose work gloves

Hearing protection to AS/NZS 1270:2002, with the class selected under AS/NZS 1269.3:2005 from the measured noise level in that plant room and recorded against the site. Do not over-protect: a class that cuts out the pump note, the alarm and an approaching vehicle takes away the hearing a lone worker depends on

Lone-worker duress device with man-down and an automatic overdue alarm — MANDATORY for any basement, plant room or riser visit, carried on the body and active, not in the bag. If a working device is not available, the visit is not a lone visit
Personal CO monitor for any after-hours or closed-up basement carpark visit, switched on and clipped at chest height
Satellite messenger only where the work is in the open air and cellular coverage is poor — it needs sky and does not work below ground
training: General construction induction training card (white card), current and not lapsed — required for construction work under ss 316 and 317 of the Regulation, and s 317(1)(b) means a card completed more than 2 years ago only stands if you have carried out construction work in the last 2 years

QBCC fire protection occupational licence in the class covering the work — Fire protection—water-based fire system—install and maintain for hydrant, booster and sprinkler servicing; Fire protection—electrical—install and maintain—fire alarm systems for detection work (maintain includes inspect and test)

Current TMR traffic management accreditation for the work being done: the implementation accreditation to place signs and devices in the road reserve, and separate traffic controller accreditation to work a stop-slow bat. CONFIRM BEFORE DISPATCH — Queensland's temporary traffic management framework, the accreditation names, the units of competency behind them and the card validity period have been in transition, and this statement deliberately does not print a unit code or a card life it could not confirm on the day it was issued. Get the current names and codes from TMR and record them against the technician
A lone technician cannot control traffic and do the work at the same time, so any job that needs a stop-slow bat is a two-person job (Step 7) — book it, do not attempt it

Current first aid and CPR: Provide First Aid refreshed every three years, Provide CPR refreshed every twelve months. Confirm the current unit codes at renewal rather than relying on the code printed on an old certificate
The company's lone worker procedure, practised and not just read: setting and holding a check-in, the overdue escalation, and using the duress device including the man-down function
Open Queensland driver licence, plus the company's carpark, ramp and reversing familiarisation — including knowing your vehicle's measured overall height with the rack, ladder and beacon on it

This SWMS read and understood before the work starts, and signed as the company's record that the arrangements required by s 300(1) are in place. s 300 does not itself require a signature — it requires the work to be carried out this way, and requires it to stop if it is not

steps.step: Plan the day, the roster and the check-in before leaving the depot
hazards: Nobody knows which site the technician is on, or which level
A fall or a collapse in a basement goes unnoticed until the next shift
A booster job on an arterial planned into the peak
Fatigue: long shifts, back-to-back night call-outs, and the drive home at 2am
A job dispatched as a lone visit that is not one — a lane-occupying zone, a confined space, work above 2 m, or a two-person lift

controls.control: Plan the exposure out before it exists. Choose the access and the method that let the whole job be done behind the kerb line, out of live aisles and off the ground: ground-level test points, an extension pole, the quiet window, the loading zone instead of the ramp. Where the frontage is an arterial with no shoulder and no safe kerb-side working space, it is not a lone job at any hour — it is booked as a crewed night shift.

Screen every job against the four things a lone technician cannot do, before it is dispatched: no device placed in a trafficked lane, no confined space entry, no work where a fall of more than 2 m is possible, no lift that needs two people. If the job needs any of them, it goes out crewed. That decision is made in the office, not at B3 at 6am.
Where the site record flags no reception in the basement, either send two people or arrange for the building manager to stand by. The flag exists so this decision is made in the office.
Book carpark and booster work into the building's quiet window — after the morning peak, before school pick-up.
Log the day's sites and the expected finish time in the app before leaving. Set the check-in interval: 60 minutes on a normal site, 30 minutes in a basement, plant room or riser.
Name the person who holds the check-in and their mobile number — a person, not 'the office'. If that person goes into a meeting, the check-in is handed over by name.

Agree the overdue action before the ute moves: one missed check-in is a call to the technician, two is a call to the building manager to have the carpark walked, then 000 with the street address and the last known level. It is not invented on the night.

Fatigue, and these are limits, not guidance. No shift longer than 12 hours including travel. At least 10 hours clear between finishing one shift and starting the next. No more than two consecutive nights of after-hours call-out, and the supervisor checks the roster for back-to-backs before dispatching — that check is the supervisor's job, not the technician's. After any call-out that finishes after midnight, or any shift past 12 hours, you do not drive home without a 20-minute break off your feet and a call to the supervisor; if you are still not right to drive, the company pays for the taxi or the room. Saying you are too tired to drive is an approved outcome and nobody is questioned for it.

Stop-work rule, agreed now so it does not have to be argued at 6am. If the work cannot be done the way this statement says — no Traffic Guidance Scheme, no permit, no lighting, no reception and no working duress device, the bay occupied, a headroom you do not fit under, a pit that would have to be entered — you stop, ring the supervisor, and do not resume until it can be done as written. s 300(2) requires exactly that, and it is the point of the whole document.

steps.step: Arrive, look at the carpark before driving into it, and park
hazards: Driving down a blind ramp into an aisle
Headroom bars and low soffits catching the ladder or the roof rack
Vehicles reversing out of bays with no warning
Reversing the ute with no spotter — the one control most reversing procedures rely on does not exist on a lone visit
Parking so the ute becomes the obstruction
A frontage or a carpark that does not feel safe to be alone in

controls.control: Park in the visitor bay or the loading zone at ground level and walk the gear in. Most fire equipment in a basement is carried to, not driven to — taking the ute down the ramp buys ten metres and a headroom problem.
Park so the vehicle is out of the live aisle: in a marked bay or hard against a wall, nose out, hazards on, amber beacon running. Never straddling a traffic lane or a ramp.

The vehicle's measured overall height, with the roof rack, ladder and beacon on it, is decalled on the A-pillar where the driver reads it at the ramp head, and the ute carries a height stick. A number on the pillar is a physical fact; a remembered height is not. If the decal is missing or the load has changed, measure it before you drive anywhere near a basement.
Use the reversing camera and sensors where the vehicle has them, and raise it as a fleet defect when they stop working. They shorten the blind spot; they do not replace getting out and looking.

Read the headroom sign against the decalled vehicle height standing at the top of the ramp, not halfway down it. AS/NZS 2890.1:2004 sets the clearance the carpark was built to — your ladder was not part of that calculation. If the two numbers are close, you do not chance it: park up top and carry.
Reverse-park on arrival wherever it is possible, so leaving is always a forward movement.

There is no spotter on a lone visit, so the reversing rule is different. Before any reverse — onto a frontage, down a ramp, out of a bay — walk the full path and look at it, then get straight back in and reverse slowly with the window down. If you cannot see the whole path from the seat, you do not reverse: you get out and look again, or you take the longer forward route.
Drive the ramp at walking pace, window down, radio off. Sound the horn at blind corners where the convex mirror is missing, fogged or aimed at nothing — and raise the mirror as a defect on the job.

If the site feels unsafe — people loitering in the carpark, a rough frontage after dark, lighting out across the whole level — leave and call the supervisor. Walking away is an approved outcome and the supervisor reschedules it with a second person. Working alone in a dark basement is a psychosocial hazard in its own right and is managed, not endured.
Class D/N vest on before the door opens, not after.

steps.step: Prove the basement will stay ventilated, and manage the heat, before you commit to working below ground
hazards: Carbon monoxide and vehicle exhaust accumulating in a basement with the carpark exhaust fans off or on a reduced after-hours cycle — which is exactly when a lone technician is there
Mechanical ventilation interlocked with the fire system, so the isolation you place stops the fans you are relying on
Heat in a closed basement, and a pump room that is hotter again with the pump running, in long-sleeve hi-vis
CO and heat both take your judgement before they take your consciousness, so a lone worker will not self-rescue

controls.control: Do not work in a closed-up basement with the carpark exhaust fans off. If they cannot be run for the visit, the visit does not happen then — it moves to a time they run, or it goes out crewed.

Before you go down, confirm with the building manager that the carpark mechanical ventilation will run for the whole visit, and that nothing you are about to isolate on the fire system will stop it. Where a ventilation or smoke-control fan test forms part of the service, run the fans while you are below ground and leave the shutdown test until you are back at ground level.

Personal CO monitor switched on and clipped at chest height for any after-hours or closed-up basement visit. In alarm you leave — immediately, by the nearest stair, not after you finish the device you are on. No monitor in the ute is not a reason to go down anyway: without one you do not work in a closed basement after hours, you ring the supervisor and it is rebooked.
Carry your water in with you, the same way the first aid kit comes in with you. Two litres for a plant room shift, on the floor beside you, not two levels up in the ute.

Cap continuous time in a hot plant room alone at 45 minutes, then out to cooler air for 10. With the pump running that is a hard limit, not a target — set the timer on the phone at the same time you set the check-in.

Headache, nausea, confusion, cramping, or not being able to hold a thought: that is a leave-immediately trigger, not something to push through. Get to open air at the ramp head, ring the check-in holder and tell them what happened. If you are alone and feeling that, you are already past the point where you would notice yourself getting worse.

steps.step: Prove the lighting before working in the basement
hazards: Sensor lighting that drops out the moment you stop moving
Unlit stairwells and ramps
Trip hazards, open pit lids, standing water, kerbs and wheel stops
Not seeing an approaching vehicle in a dim aisle
Misreading a gauge or a label in bad light

controls.control: Get the carpark and stair lighting put on permanent override for the visit. Once it is on, the override is the control — the whole level is lit for the whole job, whether or not you are moving.

Where no override is available, set the rechargeable work light at the work position before starting. Movement-sensor lighting is not lighting you can rely on: it goes out at the exact moment you stop moving, which is the moment you are concentrating on a gauge with both hands full.
Ask the building manager for the override at the pre-start call, not when you are already at B3 with the lights going out. Record who you asked and what they said.
Walk the route with the torch before carrying anything: ramps, speed humps, wheel stops, pit lids, standing water, and any bay where a parked car sits over the device you came for.

Raise lighting that is out as a defect on the job, with a photo, not as a mental note. A level that cannot be lit is a reason to reschedule with a second person, and the record is what makes that happen.
Head torch on and a charged spare hand torch in the bag. Two light sources, because the failure you are planning for is being in the dark with an injury.

steps.step: Prove communications before going where there is no reception
hazards: No phone reception in a basement, riser or plant room
A check-in that cannot be made, so the escalation fires for no reason — or does not fire when it should
An injured technician who cannot call for help and cannot be found
The office knowing the street address but not the level

controls.control: Lone-worker duress device with man-down and an automatic overdue alarm, carried on the body and active for the whole visit. The DEVICE is the control; testing it at the top of the ramp before you descend is only the check. No working device means no lone visit — ring the supervisor and it goes out crewed.

Underground the device has to work with no bars and no sky, so pick one that does: a UHF handheld or two-way radio on the building's own system, paired with the concierge or building control room; a duress pendant that relays through a base station or through a phone left at the ramp head where there is coverage. A satellite messenger needs sky — it is for open-air frontage work and is decoration on B3. Find out at this site what actually gets a signal out, and record it against the site.

Make the call from the last point where reception was good on the way in, and say where you are going and when you will be back out: 'going down to B3 plant room, out by 10:20'. That single sentence is what a search would otherwise have to guess.

Where the basement has no reception at all and the work runs longer than the check-in interval, tell the building manager or the concierge in person which level you are going to and when you are due back, and confirm face to face on the way out. A human being who expects you back is the strongest control in this step and it costs one minute.

Check the phone at the actual work position at the start. No bars means the check-in interval is no longer protecting you, and what is left is the duress device and the person who expects you back — so both of them have to be real before you go down.

Find where reception comes back — usually the ramp head, the stair core or the lift lobby — and treat that as the place you walk to in order to call. Do not prop a fire door open to get a signal: that defeats the compartmentation you are on site to maintain.

This is the s 48 control. The Regulation requires a system of work that includes effective communication with the worker, and a phone with no coverage is not one. If there is no working duress device and no person on site who expects you back, say so and stop — that is the s 300(2) stop, not a judgement call.

steps.step: Set up at a booster on a road frontage — what a LONE technician may do
hazards: Struck by a vehicle while kneeling at the booster
A driver who never sees a technician below bonnet height
Opening the ute door into a live traffic lane
Bags, drums and hose across a public footpath
Cyclists and e-scooters on the footpath or shared path behind you at 20–25 km/h, near-silent, not addressed by a vehicle scheme and not warned by a beacon aimed at the road
Being tempted to step into the lane 'just for a second' to place one cone

controls.control: A lone technician works behind the kerb line. Where the booster can be serviced entirely from behind the kerb, with no part of you and no part of the equipment in a trafficked lane, do exactly that and set no lane zone at all. Most booster services on a suburban frontage are this job.

If any part of the work, or any part of the zone the Traffic Guidance Scheme requires, reaches into a trafficked lane, you do not start. Not a cone, not a sign, not a foot. Ring the supervisor and it is rebooked as a crewed shift under Step 7. Placing a taper is itself work on foot in a live lane before any protection exists — it is the most exposed moment of the whole job and it is never a one-person task.

Behind the kerb, still build a zone: cones or a barrier along the traffic side between you and the lane, the work vehicle parked upstream of you where the frontage allows it, and a device on the FOOTPATH approach as well as the road approach. Treat a footpath, bikeway or shared path as a second traffic direction with its own approach to be warned.

Amber beacon running the whole time you are out of the vehicle, positioned to be seen from the road approach — plus a second device, a cone or a portable light, on the path approach the beacon does not cover.

Work facing the traffic. Never step backwards into a lane. Set the tablet and the torch where you do not have to turn your back to the road to read them, and check BOTH directions, road and path, before you stand up or step back — the instruction to face the traffic puts your back to the cyclists.
Get in and out of the ute on the kerb side. If it is parked so you cannot, it is parked wrong — move it before you unload.
Council or TMR road corridor permit open on the tablet before the first device goes out, wherever the zone occupies any part of the road reserve or the footpath.
Class D/N garment to AS/NZS 4602.1:2011 for the whole time inside the zone, including the walk back to the ute for a spanner.

steps.step: TWO-PERSON WORK ONLY — a work zone that occupies a trafficked lane. A lone technician does not do this step; it is here so everyone can see what the crewed version looks like and why the lone visit stops at Step 6
hazards: Struck by a vehicle while placing, adjusting or retrieving devices on foot in a live lane
A taper or advance warning set to the wrong spacing for the posted speed
One person trying to control traffic and do the work at the same time
The zone left half-picked-up after dark

controls.control: Do the work outside the lane if there is any way to: from behind the kerb, from a properly closed footpath, or under a full closure at a time the road can carry it. A lane-occupying zone is the last option, not the first.

Set the zone to the approved Traffic Guidance Scheme prepared for this site: advance warning at the spacing the scheme gives for the posted speed, the taper at the length the scheme specifies, and the work vehicle parked upstream of the work area as the shadow. Two accredited people, one placing and one watching the traffic, and the devices go out from the safe side working with the flow.
Amber beacon or truck-mounted flashing arrow running and facing the approach direction the whole time the zone is out.

The scheme is prepared by an accredited traffic management designer and every spacing comes from it, not from judgement on the day. Before relying on it, confirm with TMR which temporary traffic management framework is current for the Queensland road reserve — see the references, where that is flagged as unconfirmed at the date this statement was issued. No scheme means no zone and no job.
Traffic control with a stop-slow bat is a separate accredited person doing nothing else. Nobody holds a bat and services a booster.
Road corridor permit from council or TMR in hand before the first device goes out, and the pack-up is planned before the set-up starts (Step 13).
Class D/N garments to AS/NZS 4602.1:2011 on both people, the whole time, including the pack-up.

steps.step: Service the booster, the hydrants and the carpark devices
hazards: Stored pressure still in the booster body, the line and behind the cap after the valve is shut — a shut valve is not a dead line
A cap or a valve gland released against residual pressure becoming a projectile
A hydrant discharge running across a footpath, a shared path or a traffic lane
Kneeling head-down in a live aisle with your back to traffic
Booster cabinet doors that drop, seized caps that need a long bar, and gear carried up a fire stair when the lift is out — with nobody to take the other end
Pump room noise while the pump runs

controls.control: Isolate, lock and tag before anything is opened. Name the point on the job before you touch it — the booster isolation valve, or the section stop valve in the valve room — record its position before and after, and fit your own lock and a danger tag with your name and mobile number on it. On a lone visit nobody is watching that valve for you, so before you start, find out who else on site holds a key to it and tell them what you have done and when you will be finished.

Then take the pressure out, because isolation on its own does not. Drain or vent to a safe point — away from the road, away from the footpath, away from any electrical equipment — and prove zero on the gauge before a cap or a gland is touched.

Aim any discharge away from the road, the footpath and any shared path, into a drain or a grassed area. A flow test that puts water across a traffic lane creates the exact hazard the work zone was set up to prevent, on a surface that was dry when the driver last looked.

Crack the cap slowly and from the side, with your body and your face out of line with it, even after the gauge has read zero. If it will not move by hand and needs a bar, stop: that is a two-person job, so it is deferred and flagged on the job, not forced.

Manual handling with no second pair of hands: 20 kg is the single-person limit on this work. Above that, use the trolley or the lifting aid. Anything that needs two people — a booster cabinet door that drops when the hinge lets go, a full drum, gear up a fire stair with the lift out — is not attempted alone. It is deferred, noted on the job and rebooked with a second person. There is no team lift available to you, and that makes the limit more important here, not less.
One task out at a time. Bags, drums and the flow gauge stay inside the zone or behind the kerb line, never spread along a public footpath.

Work facing the traffic direction at the frontage; in the carpark, work facing the aisle the cars come from. Do the paperwork on the kerb side, not the traffic side — reading a tablet is exactly when you stop watching the road.

Eye protection to AS/NZS 1337.1:2010 and gloves for caps and glands, worn after the line is drained and proved and not instead of draining it. Hearing protection on before the pump starts, at the class recorded for that plant room.

steps.step: Reach a carpark detector, head or device off a ladder or a platform
hazards: Falling onto concrete, alone, in a basement with no reception — the single most likely way this activity kills someone
A ladder standing in an aisle a vehicle can reverse into
Over-reaching sideways to save moving the ladder
Nobody to foot the ladder, steady the platform or raise the alarm
Ladder feet on oil, on a ramp grade, or half on a speed hump or a wheel stop

controls.control: Do it from the ground wherever the device allows: an extension pole for a detector test, a drop-rod, a functional test from the panel. Ground level is the only fall control that never fails.

Work where a fall of more than 2 m is possible is not done on a lone visit. On this statement you work from a platform step ladder within its rated standing height and no higher, never off the top two steps, and never off a leaning ladder. Anything higher goes to a crewed visit under the working-at-height SWMS, where s 79(3) sets the order — a fall prevention device first, then a work positioning system, then a fall arrest system. A fall arrest harness is not the answer for a lone technician anyway: there is nobody to rescue you off it, and hanging in it is its own emergency.

Cone the ladder base and the aisle either side of it before the first step, and put the work vehicle between the ladder and the approach where the aisle is long. If the bay cannot be coned off, the device waits for the quiet hour or for a crew — a ladder in an aisle a vehicle can reverse into is not made acceptable by anything.

Use a platform step ladder with a handrail and a standing platform — that is the fall prevention device — set on level, solid ground with the spreaders locked and the feet clean and dry. Not on a ramp grade, not straddling a wheel stop, not on a speed hump.
Three points of contact going up and down. Keep your belt buckle between the stiles — move the ladder rather than reach for it. Tools go up in a bag or on a lanyard, not in your hand.

Tell the check-in holder before you go up and again when you are down, on any ladder work below ground. Of everything in this statement this is the task most likely to leave you on the floor unable to call.
Class D/N hi-vis so the ladder reads as a work zone rather than an obstacle, and boots with the grease wiped off the soles before the first step.

steps.step: Recognise a confined space — pits, wells and tank hatches — and stay out of it
hazards: Booster and hydrant pits, water tank hatches, pump wells, sumps and some valve rooms meeting the definition of a confined space
Oxygen deficiency or accumulated gas in a pit that has been shut since the last service
Reaching in past the point where you could get yourself back out
Drowning, entrapment or engulfment in a wet pit or a well
An open pit lid left unattended in a carpark

controls.control: No confined space entry on a lone visit. No exception, no 'just my head and shoulders', no reaching in past the point where you could get yourself back out under your own power. Before anyone enters, the Regulation requires continuous communication with the worker from outside the space and a standby person in the vicinity of it (part 4.3, s 69). Alone there is nobody to be that person, so the entry is neither lawful nor survivable, and no amount of being careful changes it.
Do the work from outside the space: read the valve, the gauge or the level from the surface, use a pole or a camera, or leave it. If it cannot be done from outside, it is not this job today.

Any pit lid or hatch you open, you barricade before you open it, and you close or cover it before you move away from it. An open pit in a carpark is a fall hazard for you and for a resident who has never looked down.

Know what counts on this work: booster and hydrant pits, water tank hatches, pump wells, sumps, and valve rooms with one small access and no ventilation. If you are not sure whether something is a confined space, treat it as one and ring the supervisor — that call takes a minute and it is always the right call.

Route the work to a crewed visit under the confined space SWMS, with an entry permit, atmospheric testing and a standby person (Regulation part 4.3). Flag it on the job with a photo so it is scheduled properly rather than left for the next lone technician to discover.

steps.step: Move around the carpark while vehicles are moving
hazards: Reversing vehicles — the driver is looking at bay numbers, not for a person
Blind aisles and missing or fogged convex mirrors
Walking behind a car with its reversing lights on
Being read as another pedestrian rather than a work zone
A resident or a driver confronting you about a coned bay, a blocked aisle or a car they cannot get past — with no colleague to de-escalate alongside you and no witness

controls.control: Cone the working area properly: the working bay and the aisle either side of it, at least two cones upstream and two downstream, and the work vehicle or a barrier between you and the approach where the aisle is long and straight.
Amber beacon running on the parked vehicle. In a dim carpark it is the only thing that reads as 'work in progress' rather than 'someone getting into their car'.

Or come back in the building's quiet hour. Scheduling does not eliminate the aisle — cars can still come down it — but it takes most of them out of the time you are standing in it. Work with the building's pattern: plant room and risers through the morning and evening peaks, aisles in the quiet hour between them.
Assume the driver has not seen you. Make eye contact before crossing behind any car with its reversing lights on, and wait for it. Hi-vis is not a right of way.

Do not argue over a bay or an aisle. If a resident or a driver fronts you, disengage: move to the vehicle or to a populated area and ring the building manager to deal with their own resident — they own that relationship, you do not. Then tell the supervisor and record it on the job. A site with repeated confrontations needs a second person or a different time slot, and the record is what gets you one.
Class D/N hi-vis in the carpark, not only on the street. Carpark lighting is worse than street lighting and the driver's eyes have not adjusted coming down the ramp.

steps.step: If it goes wrong — an injury, or a check-in you cannot make
hazards: Injured alone with no reception and nobody expecting you
An ambulance that cannot find a basement address or get past a boom gate
The lift going to fire mode with the technician on B3
A flooded road frontage becoming a public hazard

controls.control: If you are hurt and can move, get to the ramp head, the stair core or reception before you try to call. Distance to a signal beats lying where you fell hunting for a bar. If you cannot move, hit the duress button — that is what it is on your body for.

On 000, in this order: street address, then the level and the nearest column or bay number, then how the ambulance actually gets in — which entrance, whether the boom needs the building manager, whether the lift is usable. Those answers are filled into the site prompts below before the work starts, so they are read out rather than worked out.

Struck on the road frontage: LEAVE THEM WHERE THEY ARE. Put the work vehicle between them and the traffic, then call 000. Move them only if traffic is still running and cannot be stopped — and then only the shortest distance to safety.

Missed check-in: the holder rings the technician, then the building manager to have the level walked, then 000 with the address and the last known level. Nobody waits for the next check-in to see whether it clears.
Water incident at the booster or a hydrant: close the isolation valve first, then ring the building manager and the office. A flooded frontage becomes everyone's hazard within minutes.
CO monitor in alarm, or headache, nausea or confusion below ground: out by the nearest stair, into open air, then ring the check-in holder from there. Do not go back down to finish the device.

First aid kit carried in with you, not left in the ute two levels up, and checked monthly. The Regulation requires first aid equipment to be provided and every worker to have access to it — in a basement, access means on your back.

Notifiable incident — a death, a serious injury or illness, or a dangerous incident: ring the office IMMEDIATELY from site, before anything else administrative, because the Act requires the company to notify the regulator immediately on becoming aware of it and by the fastest possible means. Everything else, including near misses, goes to the office the same day.

steps.step: Pack up and clear the work zone
hazards: Struck by a vehicle while collecting cones and signs on foot — the pack-up mirrors the set-up and is just as exposed
A cone or a sign left in a lane after dark
A valve left shut, a lock left on, or a booster cap left loose
Fatigue at the end of a long solo shift

controls.control: A lone technician retrieves only what a lone technician placed: devices behind the kerb line or on a closed footpath. Nothing is picked up out of a trafficked lane by one person, ever. If the zone was a crewed zone, the crew picks it up — you do not 'just grab the last cone' on your way home.

Pick the zone up in the reverse order it went out: the devices closest to the work come up first and the advance warning comes down last, so approaching traffic is still being warned while anyone is on foot.
Count the devices out and count them back in against the scheme. A single cone left in a live lane at night is the incident.

Before leaving, walk back to every valve you touched and confirm it is in its correct position, strapped or locked, your lock and tag off you and off it, and every booster cap on and hand-tight. Record the position on the job — an unrestored valve is a defect that only shows up at a fire.

If you are running on empty at this point, stop before the drive rather than after it: the shift and rest limits in Step 1 apply to the trip home too, and the supervisor would far rather pay for a taxi than read an incident report.
Class D/N stays on until the last device is in the ute and the door is shut.

steps.responsible: Technician for a behind-the-kerb zone; Two-person crew and Supervisor for a lane zone

steps.step: Put the system back on line, clear the impairment, check out and close the job
hazards: A building left off line overnight because the closing call was never made — the most likely serious error on a lone service visit, because there is no second person to catch it
Monitoring still showing the system isolated, so a real alarm goes nowhere
Leaving site without telling the check-in holder, and a search started for someone who is already home
Site facts — lighting, reception, boom gate, plant room noise, ventilation — left in the technician's head
Driving home tired

controls.control: The impairment clearance reference and the check-out time are required fields on the close-out form — the job does not close without both, so closing the job is what forces the calls to be made rather than you remembering them at the end of a long shift. Where a build does not yet enforce it, the supervisor rejects any job closed without both, and that is checked the next morning, not at audit.
Before you leave the panel: confirm the system shows normal, that nothing you isolated is still isolated, and that every valve is back where it belongs.

Then make the one call that does both jobs: ring the monitoring company, clear the impairment, take their reference number and the time, and in that same call — or straight after — tell the building manager or the fire safety adviser the system is back on line. Write the reference number and the time on the job.

Make the check-out call to the check-in holder from the vehicle before you drive off, and say plainly that you are clear of the site. Closing the check-in is as much a control as opening it. If you are too tired to drive, say so on that call — it is an approved outcome, the same as walking away from an unsafe site, and the company pays for the break, the taxi or the room.
Sign the SWMS and the job off on the tablet at the site, while the detail is still in front of you rather than reconstructed that evening.

Record the site facts against the site: the lighting and whether an override is available, the reception dead spots and what communications actually worked down there, the boom gate arrangement and the after-hours number, the traffic peak and the quiet window, the measured noise level in the plant room, and whether the carpark ventilation runs after hours. The supervisor reads these into the review of this statement — they are the monitoring half of it.

Raise the real defects on the job with photos: failed carpark lighting, the missing convex mirror, the booster with no clearance, the frontage with no safe kerb-side working space, the pit that would have to be entered. Those are the things that make the next lone visit safer, or get it crewed.

emergency:
Call 000 first, then the office. In a basement the problem is rarely the injury — it is that nobody knows where you are.

Injured and able to move: get to the ramp head, the stair core or reception before trying to call. Do not lie where you fell hunting for a signal. If you cannot move, hit the duress button.

On 000, in this order: the street address, then the level and the nearest column or bay number, then how the ambulance gets in — which entrance, whether the boom gate needs the building manager, whether the lift is usable. Those answers are filled into the site prompts before the work starts so they can be read out, not worked out.

Struck on the road frontage: LEAVE THEM WHERE THEY ARE. Put the work vehicle between them and the traffic, then call 000. Move them only if traffic is still running and cannot be stopped — and then only the shortest distance to safety.

Missed check-in: the check-in holder rings the technician, then the building manager to have the level walked, then 000 with the site address and the last known level. Nobody waits for the next interval to see if it clears.

Water incident at the booster or a hydrant: shut the booster isolation valve or the section stop valve, then call the building manager and the office. A flooded frontage is a public hazard within minutes.

CO monitor in alarm, or headache, nausea or confusion below ground: leave immediately by the nearest fire stair, get to open air, and call the check-in holder from there. Do not go back down to finish the device.

Fire alarm while you are below ground: leave by the fire stair, not the vehicle ramp, and go to the assembly area. Tell the warden or the arriving brigade that a technician was working on the system and exactly what is isolated.

REPORTING. A notifiable incident — a death, a serious injury or illness, or a dangerous incident — is rung through to the office IMMEDIATELY from site, before anything else administrative. The Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) requires the company to notify the regulator immediately on becoming aware of a notifiable incident, by the fastest possible means: Workplace Health and Safety Queensland, 1300 362 128. The office cannot do that if you hold the report until the end of the day. Every other incident and every near miss goes to the office the same day.

AFTER A NOTIFIABLE INCIDENT. The site must not be disturbed until an inspector arrives, or until an inspector directs otherwise (WHS Act s 39). That duty sits on whoever has management or control of the workplace, which in somebody else's building is normally the building owner or manager — so tell the building manager as well as the office, and tell them why. You may still act to help an injured person, to remove a deceased person, to make the site safe or to prevent another incident, or as police direct. The office keeps a record of the notifiable incident for at least 5 years.

siteSpecificPrompts: Who holds your check-in today — name and mobile — and at what interval? What is the agreed overdue trigger time?
Which levels, bays or column numbers are you working at today? This is what gets read out to 000.
Where does phone reception come back in this building — the ramp head, the stair core, the lift lobby, the street?
Is your duress device charged, paired and tested today — and what actually relays a signal out of this building's basement? (Radio to the concierge, a base station, a phone at the ramp head?)
How does an ambulance get in? Which entrance, does the boom gate need the building manager or a fob, and what is the after-hours number?
Is the carpark lighting on movement sensors, and who can put it on permanent override for this visit?
Does the carpark mechanical ventilation run at the time of your visit, and will anything you isolate on the fire system stop it? Who confirmed that, and when?
What is the measured noise level in this plant room, and what class of hearing protector does that give under AS/NZS 1269.3? Record it once for the site rather than guessing it each visit.
What is the headroom at the ramp, and does the ute fit with the ladder and beacon on the roof? What does the A-pillar decal say?
What is this carpark's traffic peak, and what quiet window has the building manager given you?
Does any part of the work or the work zone touch the road reserve or the footpath? If so, is the council or TMR road corridor permit in hand?
Is there an approved Traffic Guidance Scheme for this frontage, and who prepared it? Does it put any device in a trafficked lane — because if it does, today is not a lone visit?
Does the frontage have a footpath, bikeway or shared path behind the booster, and which way do cyclists and scooters come from?
Which devices at this site need a ladder, and can any of them be reached from the ground instead? Is a fall of more than 2 m possible at any of them — because if it is, that device is not done today?
Are there pits, tank hatches, pump wells or sumps in scope here? None of them are entered on a lone visit — will any of the work need one opened?
Where is the booster isolation valve or the section stop valve, who else on site holds a key to it, and where is the drain or vent point you will prove at zero?
What is the monitoring company's number and the site or account reference you will need to place and then clear the impairment?
What time did you start, when did you last finish, and are you inside the shift and rest limits in Step 1? Is tonight a second consecutive night call-out?
Is a building manager or concierge on site today, and have you told them in person which level you are going to and when you are due back?
